    This wasn’t bratty Rio, or even righteous Rio.

    This was something else.

    Darker. Unleashed.

    And it turned her on more than she could admit, even to herself.

    Agatha had always been drawn to the writer’s smugness, but this felt like something deeper cracking open.

    A glimpse of something deeper, wilder, that had always been there - just waiting to be seen. Rio, painfully aware of the effect she was having on the drama queen in heels who kept pushing her luck, gave a slow half-shrug. Cool, controlled. Casual in the way a tiger might flick its tail before pouncing.

    “What’s wrong?” she asked “Didn’t expect the puppy to grow teeth?”

    The Head Producer said nothing. Her brain scrambled for footing, for an angle. None came. She was drowning in a Rio she didn’t recognize - and couldn’t stop looking at. Her not-so-disposable asset took a half-step closer, her presence magnetic, merciless. “Look at you, skimming for your next line.” she continued, smirking now “If you had a mustache, you’d be twirling it right now.”

    Agatha’s lips parted - reflex, not intention - but the brown-eyed fantasy cut her off before a single syllable could land. Her breath hit her cheek as she leaned in, close enough to make retreat impossible without humiliation.

    “So go ahead, Agatha. What’s the magic line?” Rio inisisted, voice low and close and intimate in the worst possible way. “What’s the brilliant fucking monologue that buys you another night with me? What string of words will sweep it all under the rug so you can keep fucking me like it means nothing?”

    Agatha’s breath caught.. Audible.

    * Who was this woman? *

    This wasn’t the Rio she’d come to count on - the one with the easy warmth, the reckless generosity, the golden heart that had followed her around like a codependent emotional support animal. Too loyal. Too available. Always ready to absorb the fallout. No. This woman with hypnotic serial killer eyes was new. Or maybe not new at all. Maybe this had always been inside her, locked behind that soft exterior. The precision. The anger. The control. The goddamn power of it all.

    Rio had always been the sweet one. Gentle. Patient. Almost pathologically understanding. But this version?

    She was throwing Agatha so off balance she didn’t know whether to run, fight, or beg. And Agatha Harkness - Agatha fucking Harkness - did not get thrown. Not like this. Not by anyone.

    She tried to recalibrate.

    Too late.

    Rio was already speaking again, the blade of her voice cutting deeper with each pass. “You saw the golden retriever and figured you’d just reap the benefits.” she muttered bitterly, gesturing to herself “You thought I’d keep wagging my tail, licking your hand, begging for scraps. No matter what.”

    “I never thought that” Agatha’s voice cracked just enough to betray her. It was true. She hadn’t thought that. Not consciously. But the truth was irrelevant now. Rio wasn’t letting her off the hook.

    The ocean-eyes mess took a half-step back. Not a retreat, exactly, but her ass hit the desk behind her, and Rio clocked it instantly.

    “And now” she said, advancing. Furious. “You thought if you pushed hard enough, if you trapped me here, forced my hand, I’d come crawling back. Like a good little secret. Back to your bed, back to your rules. Like nothing ever fucking happened.”

    Agatha opened her mouth, then closed it again. The lump in her throat wouldn’t budge. The air between them vibrated with something unstable. Hot. Unmanageable. Her latest addiction stepped in even closer - too close. Agatha could smell her now. Skin and heat and fury, a scent she knew too well and craved like nicotine.

    “Are you seriously turned on right now?” Rio laughed. Dry. Contemptuous. Agatha’s eyes dropped to her lips - instinct again - and that was all her ex lover needed to confirm the answer.

    “Unbelievable” she muttered. Now her arms were braced on either side of Agatha’s hips, palms flat on the desk where the big boss was half-sitting, half-clinging, spine arched in self- defense or surrender.

    She didn’t know which.

    Her body didn’t either.

    The desk creaked beneath her, a soft groan of protest that seemed to echo the strain in her muscles.

    Her breath barely registered. Her legs didn’t feel real anymore. Damn, her whole body didn't feel real anymore.

    She couldn’t - for the life of her - think straight. Stuck in that trembling space between ' don’t you ever fucking look at me again' and ' hold me close and never let me go' . At this point Agatha’s ass was literally on top of the desk. All she could do was lean back - just slightly, instinctively - as if even an inch of distance might help her breathe. Her palms pressed into the wood, knuckles whitening, eyes helplessly locked on Rio’s mouth. She tried to rally. To summon every trick in her book - every flirt, every smirk, every little charm that had ever worked on Rio before.

    But her favorite mistake wasn’t biting. Those furious, exquisite lips kept moving - each disdain-laced word landing like a bruise.

    “I know that needy, greedy look” she whispered, now close enough to steal breath. Agatha's spine arched so far back she could feel the cool edge of the monitor pressing into her shoulder blades.

    Rio wasn’t teasing. Not this time.

    Her voice had dipped into something lower and rougher. A frequency reserved for trouble. “You’re thinking about doing something filthy to me” she said Breathing was suddenly a skill the self-sabotage queen no longer possessed. Rio's mouth curled into something dark.“Or maybe it’s the other way around.” Her tone shifted again - wicked, certain.

    “Maybe what you really want… what you need… is for me to do something filthy to you.” Agatha’s fingers dug into the desk even more, breath coming short and useless, like her lungs were stuck trying to catch a memory.

    Rio leaned closer, until every syllable landed against her lips, vibrating with the weight of unspoken things.

    “If I were you” she threatened quietly “I wouldn’t keep me here against my will.” The words sliced clean.

    No dramatics.

    Just truth, weaponized.

    Agatha felt the cut long after Rio had finished speaking. Her breath faltered, caught between the inhale and the exhale, a shallow tide she didn’t remember choosing. Her chest rose, fell. Again.

    “I don’t have a choice” she murmured, more to herself than to Rio. Her voice sounded distant, like it was being funneled through water. Like she was hearing it from the end of a tunnel she no longer controlled.

    Somewhere between confrontation and collapse, Agatha had slipped into a state she didn’t understand - a strange kind of subspace where dominance and submission blurred into something almost spiritual.

    Without fully realizing it, she lifted both hands - her left tucking a strand of hair behind her ear, and her right mirroring the motion on the other side.

    It was a small gesture. Automatic. Fragile. Almost unconscious.

    Both hands moved with a shaky kind of grace, smoothing her hair back until it lay parted and flat, leaving her face completely exposed - like a girl about to confess something she hadn’t yet found the courage to say out loud.

    The sight of it - so vulnerable and unguarded - stopped Rio cold.

    She’d never seen her do that.

    Not once.

    And it undid something in her.

    It yanked her straight out of the high she’d been riding - out of the dominance that had crackled through her like electricity just moments earlier - and left her staring at something she hadn’t known she craved: Agatha, off-balance.

    Agatha twitching with nerves, like she didn’t know whether to run or beg. It was, without question, the hottest fucking thing she had ever seen. A fucking whole new level of irresistible.

    Her pulse spiked.

    * If only I’d dragged that out of her sooner. *

    She would’ve used it. Exploited it. Savored it.

    Loved it - in a very...specific way.

    Her pupils dilated, blown wide with want. Her stance remained taunt, coiled. The fury inside her didn’t vanish - but it bent. Slightly. The edge dulled.

    Not her control.

    And definitely not the animosity still surging toward the woman in front of her. There was something devastating about the way they burned toward each other. Two forces that shouldn’t touch - yet always did.

    Obsession dressed up as intimacy. Violence masquerading as desire.

    They didn’t love each other in any way that made sense.

    But it was real.

    And it was terrifying.

    In another life, maybe they’d have been gentle with each other.

    But not in this one.

    “Then, I guess I’ll have no choice but to teach you a lesson”

    Rio's hands rose with eerie calm. She cupped her beautiful past craving's face like it was something valuable, irreplaceable. Her thumbs brushed delicately over her cheekbones, then slowly – intentionally - tucked those same strands of hair back out from behind Agatha’s ears. One side. Then the other.

    She was undoing her defenses. Quietly. Sweetly. Like unwrapping something she intended to break.

    Her voice dropped into something dangerously soft. “Are you even ready for that? Do you have any idea what you're about to set off?”

    Agatha stared up at her, lips parted, eyes wide.

    No.

    She didn’t care.

    She didn’t even know what Rio meant.

    She was too far gone.

    But muscle memory kicked in - just long enough for her to recover a fragment of the tone that had built an empire and bulldozed more than one lover into submission. “Just sign the contract” she snapped. It wasn’t a request. It was an attempt at escape - a fast- forward button, pressed hard, hoping to skip the wreckage and land squarely in victory. But Rio didn’t move.

    One hand braced on the desk, beside Agatha’s hip. The other stayed exactly where it was - cupping her jaw like something she might shatter if she squeezed too hard. Thumb pressing just beneath the hinge of her cheekbone, mapping bone and skin as if reading some secret code embedded in her face.

    It wasn’t a caress.

    It was a diagnosis.

    “I wonder if anyone’s ever tightened the screws on you, Ms. Harkness.” Rio said quietly, voice electric and low “Really made you feel it. Not just punished you, but made you understand.”

    Agatha flinched - but only slightly. Enough for her former lover to catch it. Enough to give her leverage.

    “It’s just Agatha” she replied, brittle, straining for nonchalance and failing. “I figured you’d screamed it out loud enough times to have it memorized by now.”

    Once, back when she felt connected to Rio, Ms. Harkness had sounded like flirtation - an inside joke laced with innuendo. Now it felt like a sentence. Formal, final. A wall. “That was before. This mean girl act?” Rio's eyes narrowed. “It has consequences.” Agatha's expression tilted somewhere between amusement and disbelief. She tried to laugh. It got stuck halfway out of her throat. A hiccup of air. A sound that couldn’t commit to what it wanted to be.

    Still, her mouth curved - barely. Bratty. Breathless.

    “What are you gonna do?” she muttered, voice thin and rising. “Write me a strongly worded essay?”

    Rio did smile then - but it was cold, bloodless.

    Not warm.

    It was the kind of smile you give someone right before you break them in half. “Since you’re a liar, it has to be something stronger than words. Something that stings.” she said “Just enough to let you feel what the rest of us carry after one of your little power plays.” Agatha’s mouth curled into a decoy expression. A ghost of bravado.

    “Well” she said, her voice cool but shaking at the edges “just bear in mind I respond better to encouragement.”

    “Then I encourage you not to suck so hard” Rio replied dryly.

    A pause. Long enough to feel like a slap in the silent room.

    Agatha insisted, voice rising: “Sign the contract, my love. So we can put all this behind us and skip straight to the kissing.”

    * Entitlement. Again *

    She was trying to reclaim the rhythm. Control the frame. Turn the whole thing back into a game she could win by sheer force of will.

    But Rio didn’t bite. Something inside her almost cracked, but the fury had calcified a few days ago. Hardened into something so dense, it couldn’t be melted. Not by sex. Not by Agatha Harkness and her impossible charm.

    She shook her head slowly, exhaling a sound that barely qualified as a laugh. Dry. Grave. A sound full of everything she wasn’t saying.

    “¡Ay, Agathita!” she murmured. Softly, almost tenderly. Devastatingly. “¿Qué voy a hacer contigo?”

    The word hit harder than it had any right to.

    * Agathita. *

    A year and a half of Spanish lessons hadn’t prepared her for this.

    The way that diminutive felt in Rio’s mouth.

    It wasn’t cruel.

    It was worse.

    It was personal. Unforgivably intimate.

    No one had ever called her that.

    No one had dared.

    It melted something inside Agatha before she could brace herself.

    The syllables hit like a wound reopening. And somewhere between her ribs and hips, something melted - unprotected, involuntary, indecent.

    Her thighs pressed together in reflex. An answer without a question. A yes without language. She stared at Rio’s lips, stunned, as if the word had been a kiss.

    Rio didn’t notice.

    Couldn’t.

    Too furious.

    Too far gone to see the way she still fractured Agatha, effortlessly, every time she opened her mouth.

    Because the truth was - they were trapped.

    Not just in this room or in this fight.

    But in a power struggle so deep-rooted, so damn inevitable, it was practically stitched into the walls.

    Infatuation had done its job. That early, disorienting high - when everything felt sacred, and time bent around their bodies - had fused them like a violent prayer. The spell hadn’t been gentle. It had scorched through their boundaries, rewired their logic, carved tunnels through their resolve. And they had loved it. They’d let it.

    But once it faded, all that remained was friction.

    The illusion of merging gave way to impact. Not soft or silent - but loud. Violent. Unrelenting. They weren’t becoming one anymore. They were colliding.

    Agatha wanted space - but only the kind where Rio chased her across it. Rio wanted closeness - but only if she didn’t have to vanish inside of it. They both wanted to be understood - but only through their own language, on their own terms.

    They both wanted transformation - not of themselves, but of each other. They wanted their lover reshaped into the version that best served their wounds. Smoothed out. Easier to love. They knew that was toxic.

    They did it anyway.

    Because neither of them knew how to carry their own pain. So they handed it off. They turned each other into mirrors. Into battlegrounds. Into medicine. And that’s why the relationship was unraveling.

    Not because they didn’t care for each other.

    But because they did.

    That’s why Rio’s next words landed like a guillotine.

    “Is this really how you want it to end?”

    The silence that followed was vicious.

    Tense.

    Brutal.

    Agatha didn’t respond.

    She couldn’t.

    Or maybe she wouldn’t. The line between the two blurred too fast to track. Rio nodded, like she’d already accounted for the silence. Like heartbreak had been factored into the script.

    “Okay then” she said. Flat. Dead calm. “I’ll play.”

    She stepped back.

    And the heat drained from Agatha’s body like a current cut at the source - replaced by something colder. Smaller. Harder to disguise.

    The loss of proximity wasn’t the punishment.

    It was the confirmation.

    That something had shifted.

    That Rio was done making room for grace.

    The writer's voice, when it returned, had no emotion left in it.

    “Pass me the document.”

    Agatha didn’t speak. Just reached for the laptop beside her and turned it toward Rio, who signed the contract with two clicks and a drag of her finger. No hesitation. No drama. Just quiet, methodical frustration.

    She closed the laptop slowly, tucked it under her arm, and stepped forward again. Close enough for her knee to graze Agatha’s.

    Too damn close.

    And Agatha - who once would’ve leaned into it - held still. Tense. Controlled. Except for her pulse, which betrayed her completely.

    “I won’t give you what you want” Rio said. Her voice wasn’t angry. It wasn’t cold either. It was something worse. Icy with purpose. “But for the love of God, I’ll give you what you deserve.”

    She hovered there a moment. Calculating. A wolf in slow motion.

    Agatha could feel it in her chest - that primal hush before a decision. A thrill shot down her spine before she could scold herself for it.

    To top off the already surreal, almost Kafkaesque vibe of it all, her past affair's fingers closed around her jaw - precise, steady, unyielding.

    “Open your mouth.”

    The command sliced straight through her. No irony. No innuendo. No room for deflection. And somehow – somehow - Agatha obeyed.

    She wasn’t sure why. Maybe because no one had ever spoken to her like that. Maybe because the ache in her legs said do it, even when her brain screamed don’t. She kept her eyes on Rio’s, wide and unsure, lips parted, like a kid caught breaking the rules. She told herself it was a performance. Told herself it was about regaining control. But her body wasn’t listening. Her body leaned into the moment like it had been waiting for it. Rio leaned in slowly, her gaze steady, unreadable.

    For a second - just one - Agatha thought Rio was finally going to kiss her. But instead, she spit.

    Right into her mouth.

    The heat of it landed on her tongue like a brand - wet, shocking, unmistakably intimate. It slid down her throat before she could stop it.

    It was vulgar. And obscene.

    And worse.

    It was personal. A kind of vengeance that knew exactly where to land. Her mouth closed instinctively. Reflex more than decision.

    She swallowed.

    And hated how easy it was. How easily her body accepted it.

    A storm broke loose inside her - rage, lust, disbelief. Nothing landed. Everything burned. Her thighs clenched again. Her breath shallowed.

    “I guess we’re both gonna have to swallow things we don’t want to from now on.” Rio said, her voice low and final.

    And Agatha - Agatha, who’d survived boardrooms, betrayals, the press, the studio, and half the men who’d ever tried to put her in a corner - just sat there.

    Mute.

    Horny.

    Shaking.

    The taste of spit still clung to her tongue like something sacred and filthy all at once. She didn’t know what to do with it - didn’t know where to file the heat crawling up her neck or the way her body, traitorous and lit up, kept replaying the moment on a loop. Rio turned without a word. Walked away like it cost her nothing. No flare of regret. No backward glance to acknowledge she had just unraveled the most guarded woman in Westview with a gesture that was part punishment, part prophecy.

    She moved like someone who had made peace with the damage.

    At the door, she paused. Looked back once. Her expression blank in that dangerous way that meant she’d already decided what kind of story this was going to be.

    “I hope you’re ready to have someone you care for as an enemy” she said. “Because this is going to get ugly.”

    And then...

    she was gone.

    The door slammed behind her.

    Agatha, alone now, finally understood: She hadn’t just lost her. She’d lost the chance to ever get her back.

    Five hours later, the building’s alarm screamed.

    A high-pitched, annoying as hell, shrieking wail tore through the clean, tempered-glass silence of Westview Productions, jarring as a fork scraping bone. It didn’t crescendo. It hit at full volume and stayed there - merciless, industrial, pulsing through every floor with violence.

    Agatha didn’t even flinch. She didn’t even look up from her screen.

    The tension from the earlier conversation had left her too drained to stress about anything else. No alarm could compete with the internal noise she was already managing. Too much of her had already burned that morning. Her limbs felt underwater. Her skull was full of fog. The tail end of a migraine looped behind her left eye like a phantom. She figured it was a drill. Or some overeager intern waving a Juul too close to the smoke detectors on the tech floor. Maybe someone had nuked tupperware pasta again. Not that it mattered.

    She kept working - half-editing a development slate, half-humming a dumb little melody her son had made up and repeated for hours until it calcified in her mind like gum on a shoe. Something between a lullaby and a curse that she couldn’t stop humming it now even if she tried.

    Suddenly, Herbert was standing in the office doorway, panting like he’d sprinted up five flights. His button-down had sweat shadows under the arms. He clutched his phone like it was about to explode.

    “Hey, neighbor” he said, breathless. “Surprised to see you still in here. We need to evacuate.”

    “Why?”

    “They haven’t told us exactly. Just that it’s coming from the lower levels. Security’s clearing every floor.”

    Her stomach tightened.

    Normally, these kinds of alarms came from the studio lots - someone tripping over a prop, a tech glitch, a minor fire. But if it was coming from the office wing... that was different. If something had gone wrong here, it might be connected to one of the covert deals she’d brokered for Westview lately.

    It could’ve been anything.

    A leak.

    A breach.

    Too many buried things in this building. Too many files. Too many secrets she’d personally arranged to keep underground.

    “Threat level?” she asked, her voice steady.

    "It's under control. Or it will be. That's all we know" her assistant said. "Protocol still applies."

    Agatha stood - the way someone rises when called to the witness stand. She grabbed her blazer, her bag, two of her phones… and left the rest behind.

    And muttered a silent plea to the universe that this was just Dottie Jones losing it and chaining herself to a pillar in protest over god knows what.

    At least then, Agatha would know exactly where to find her.

    Now that would brighten her day.

    The stairwells buzzed with worried whispers and speculation.

    People moved in clumps, murmuring. Everyone holding their phones and glancing at their smartwatches like they were waiting for divine guidance from a group chat. Someone from Legal insisted it was a false alarm. A PA from Props claimed there’d been actual smoke. A grip from Stage A whispered the word arson with such eerie confidence that Agatha briefly wondered if he'd started it himself just for the drama.

    She ignored them all. No one here ever knew anything. Sheep, the lot of them. They exited out the main lobby, past the concierge and the art installation Agatha had always hated but approved anyway to win points with the board.

    Outside, the sun was ruthless, the heat unforgiving.

    The sky was steel, and the air carried the acidic ghost of fire. She smelled it before she saw it. And she knew. Immediately.

    It wasn’t a drill.

    Staff milled around like ants post-flood. Some stood in small groups, gossiping too loud. Others sat on the low wall around the building’s circular garden, scrolling mindlessly through social media, waiting for someone else to tell them what to feel.

    Agatha didn’t join them. She stood on the curb, back straight, eyes narrowed, arms folded. Chin tilted.

    At the fifty-minute mark, a fire truck pulled away from the garage entrance. “Another beautiful day” she said to Herbert who hovered beside her the whole time, tapping notes into his iPad as if this were just another Tuesday.

    At fifty-six, the heavy black smoke billowing from the garage began to fade into gray. And at exactly one hour, a woman in tactical black, dark sunglasses in place, approached. Early thirties. Auburn hair, perfectly styled despite the heat.

    She wore a close-cut jacket over combat-fit pants, her movement smooth, unhurried. Clipboard in one hand, comms earpiece gleaming against her temple.

    Agatha clocked her instantly. One of the top operatives from Westview's corporate security. “There’s no ongoing threat, ma'am. The building is secure.” the operative said. “But I'll need you to come with me. Down to the parking level.

    She turned her head slightly, one brow arched.

    “Why?”

    “I think it’s best if you see for yourself.”

    She nodded once and followed. No further questions.

    The elevators were still down, so they took the stairs - two flights to the sublevel. On the way, Romanoff asked if she had any known enemies - then, almost offhandedly, mentioned that the security company had been tipped off by an anonymous call. By the time they reached the bottom level, Agatha didn’t need anyone to spell it out. The smell hit her first.

    The acrid cling of something that should never have burned, but had. Melted plastic. Scorched rubber. Synthetic fumes soaked deep into concrete. It didn’t rise so much as hang in the air, heavy and sour.

    The parking garage was quiet. Still. Most of the cars sat untouched in their usual spots, framed by flickering overhead lights and the distant echo of their own footsteps. On the surface, nothing looked out of place Except for the carcass.

    She spotted it halfway across the floor.

    What remained of her Aston Martin slumped in its designated space like a dead animal - charred, hollowed out, unrecognizable. The once-sleek body was now a warped shell, blackened and blistered, its curves twisted into something grotesque. The windshield had caved inward, glass fused to metal. One side mirror dangled by a thread of melted wiring, swaying slightly in the stale air. The tires were gone, vaporized in the heat. What was left of the paint curled in sickly strips, flaking like old skin peeling from a burn. For certain angles it almost looked like a brutalist sculpture in some Berlin gallery, solemn and devastating. Something with a title like Mourning or What Remains. Thin smoke still snaked from the ruin. A hiss here. A crackle there. Not a blaze. Just the ghost of one.

    She couldn’t look away.

    Another member of the security team approached. He didn’t introduce himself. Just offered her a look that said he’d rather be doing anything else.

    The man cleared his throat. “We have footage” he said. “You ready to see it?” She didn’t nod. Just held out her hand.

    The tablet was already queued up. Security footage in full HD, flickering with grainy shadows and low light - but crystal clear where it mattered.

    “Whenever you're ready” he said.

    She pressed play.

    And there she was.

    The arsonist.

    The figure in the video moved with purpose. Hood up. Face partially obscured by a mask, but the body language was unmistakable. This person was on a mission. The gait. The posture. Hair pulled up into a messy bun. Shoulders squared like they were about to stage a revolution.

    They didn’t pause to check for cameras or look over their shoulder. No. They marched straight to the car.

    Driver’s side window: smashed with the blunt end of a fire extinguisher. Precise. Efficient.

    No hesitation. No fumbling. Just a single strike, then shaking out the shards like unboxing something they’d been waiting for.

    From the duffel on their shoulder, they pulled a plastic container - clear, industrial, sloshing with a thick amber liquid. Not gasoline. Something stickier. Meaner. Homemade. They circled the car once. Trunk. Hood. Tires. A slow pour through the shattered window onto the leather seats.

    A pause.

    Then, from a pocket: a Zippo. No flourish. No drama. Just a clean flick - open flame. They dropped it straight onto the soaked upholstery, casual as lighting a birthday candle. The ignition was instant.

    The fire didn’t erupt - it claimed. It bloomed. Bright. Hungry. Intentional. The figure stepped back just enough to avoid the worst of the heat. They watched it rise. Let it touch their face. And then - facing the nearest camera - they raised one hand and flipped it off. Middle finger. Dead center of the frame.

    Proud.

    Agatha stared at the frozen image as the video looped back to the beginning. Her own face remained still. But her fingers tightened around the tablet until the plastic creaked.

    “Do you recognize this person?” the officer asked quietly.

    She replayed the video.

    Those fingers - she would know them anywhere. The way they moved. The way they felt. The way they still haunted her skin.

    That gesture. The flick of the middle finger - not raised, but thrust outward, like an accusation.

    Even the way the arsonist body leaned ever so slightly when she walked, as if pulled by some calm gravity.

    Her mouth twitched, the tiniest betrayal of satisfaction.

    “No fucking clue” she said.

    A lie, so smooth it didn’t even register as effort.

    She turned her head slightly and glanced at what remained of the car. The metal shell had melted the license plate into a silver smudge. Her reflection rippled on the scorched surface - distorted, monstrous, mythic.

    The officer cleared his throat again. “How do you want us to handle it? Should we notify police? Legal? Someone from the board?”

    The producer didn’t answer right away. She considered the question like a philosopher considers the end of the world.

    Finally, without emotion, she said “No. I’ll handle it”

    “But, ma’am, if you don’t press charges...”

    “I said I’ll handle it” she cut him off, still calm, still level.

    * She absolutely would *

    With a slow, disdainful grace, she returned the tablet. “Erase everything. Every copy, every backup. No leaks. No traces. This never happened.”

    Then came the smile - quiet, chilling, and utterly final.

    “As far as Westview knows... this woman was never here.”

    She turned, walked away from the wreckage, and took out her phone.

    “Herbert” she said, the moment he picked up. “Spread the word: there was an electrical fault in the underground lot. A minor fire. No foul play. Faulty wiring. That’s the story. Got it?” She didn’t wait for his confirmation. She ended the call mid-breath.

    By the time she reached the end of the corridor - past the stairwell, past the last checkpoint, and the final security camera - she was alone.

    Truly alone.

    Alone with the echo of her own heels and the crackling silence that comes after something sacred has burned.

    That was the moment, and the place, where the laughter broke free.

    Not a chuckle. Not a dry, bitter exhale. Not something meant for an audience. No.

    Her head fell back.

    The sound ripped out of her - loud, low, guttural. Almost a howl. Her whole body pitched forward, hands on her knees, like it had caught her off guard. Like pleasure. Like pain. Like sex.

    A crack in her composure - wild and hot and impossible to put back.

    * This girl. Always too much *

    Rio could’ve taken the clean route. The rational one. She could’ve filed a formal complaint. Marched straight into HR. Attached receipts - screenshots, timestamps, emails, consent threads. She could’ve built a case. Presented it to the board with a bow tied around it. She could’ve dismantled Agatha Harkness like a professional.

    Quietly. Systematically.

    Like a sane person.

    But instead?

    She set Agatha’s fucking car on fire.

    She could still smell the smoke on her collar. Could taste it in the back of her throat, acrid and intimate. It clung to her hair, her skin, her clothes.

    The gesture was so reckless, so unhinged, so brutally theatrical - so deliciously unnecessary - it landed somewhere between a declaration of war and a love confession. It wasn’t just arson. It was art. A performance piece. A provocation in flame and gasoline. Because from her perspective, the fire wasn’t about destruction.

    It was communication.

    It was punishment. But also a symbol. A manifest.

    A violent, romantic act of vandalism.

    An obscene little love letter spelled out in accelerant and ash.

    Yes, it was a threat. No question.

    But also?

    It gave her hope.

    How exquisitely fucked up was that?

    On a scale from zero to completely deranged - how deeply had Agatha fallen to find this entire spectacle romantic as fuck?

    No one had ever hated her with this kind of precision before. With intent. With imagination. With flair.

    Because no one had ever wanted her enough to burn something down for her. And hate like that - that specific, cinematic kind of hate - meant unfinished business. It meant she still had a chance.

    She was surprised, honestly. Perversely impressed.

    Because Rio hadn’t just torched a car.

    She left Agatha a message.

    And Agatha understood it. Every syllable. Every note.

    She knew it the way predators know blood in the air. The way artists understand instinctively where the light will fall.

    Rio loved to brag that she’d cracked the Harkness code.

    But Agatha was fluent in Rio Vidal, too.

    And in that fire, in that final shot of her on camera - middle finger raised, unbothered, unbroken - Agatha heard it loud and clear: - I’m not done with you.-

    Her hands trembled as she reached the top of the stairs.

    And she felt...

    Relieved.

    Actually, truly, deeply relieved.

    She caught her reflection in the black glass of the lobby - wild hair, smoke-stained blouse, eyes lit with something far too close to joy - and smiled.

    Because she hadn’t lost Rio.

    Not really.

    Not yet.

    And some fires - if you know how to feed them - are better stoked than extinguished. * What bliss. What absolute, infernal bliss. *
