    Chapter 21: Perfectly Confusing, or The One Where Rio’s Logic

    and Agatha’s Intuition Refuse to Sync Chapter Summary Agatha lectures a useless, brooding Rio on the fine art of constructive anger. Chapter Notes See the end of the chapter for notes Not to be dramatic or anything, but let me ask you this again: Have you ever felt THE PROBLEM?

    Did you ever fell in love with a smug, merciless temptress?

    An apex predator who fed on being unreachable, who could strip you bare just by existing? I'm talking about a sexy fallen angel walking around in the skin of a woman named Agatha Harkness.

    A sorcerer who bent time - and you - like clay.

    Who could stretch a single night into weeks, weeks into months, months into whole years with nothing but her long, veiny, bony hand between your thighs and her maddening, hungry tongue pressed against yours.

    A woman who drained every ounce of your devotion and turned your desire into an offering laid like a sacrifice across the altar of her perfectly carved legs.

    Who hypnotized you with those ocean-witch eyes, and rewired your pulse until breathing itself felt like something she allowed.

    An electric, addictive, devastating apparition who didn’t just mark your body - she branded your mind, your soul, your fucking identity.

    Tell me - has the perfect woman ever come out of nowhere and, in a few brutal months of giving you the best sex of your life, not just consumed you but erased you? Devour everything you were and spit you back out as someone unrecognizable? Have you ever given someone that much power - that time, memory, willpower, even your sense of self - meant nothing in her hands?

    Someone who, in no time at all, made you feel a passion nobody else had touched in years. Someone so potent that character and time collapsed beside her, because with her you weren’t just different - you were someone new.

    A siren who made you dance to her rhythm. Who didn’t just promise that madness could be music, but dragged you right to the edge of insanity and made sure you heard the melody too. Did that selfish bitch keep you hidden from the world - only to throw you out of her house later, apologizing with all the sincerity of a snake while trying to chain you to her side with a job under her wing? Threats dressed up as generosity. Control dressed up as opportunity. And still - still - that same maddening woman had the audacity, in the middle of your fury, to beg you to stay.

    To beg you to kiss her.

    To call you my love.

    See? Not a problem. The problem.

    Because that was Agatha. Always a fucking problem.

    She hid Rio away. Hunted her. Pulled her close, then treated her like shit. And then she wanted to get closer all over again.

    She marked her, carved her, rewrote her from the inside out until nothing of the original was left.

    She made her feel like...

    ...like the only sane option right now would be to bury her face in a pillow and scream until her throat ripped raw.

    But what good would that do? Agatha would still be there, echoing in her bloodstream, smirking in the back of her skull.

    So let’s cut the bullshit.

    If none of this has ever happened to you - if you’ve never been chewed up, spit out, rebuilt, and possessed by a fucking succubus in human skin.

    If you’re not the kind of fucked-up freak who torched her precious car not just to teach her a lesson, but to prove you wanted more of her.

    To give her a taste of exactly what you’re planning to do to her in bed. To put her in her place.

    Then you don’t get to judge.

    You don’t get to say a single goddamn word about the choices Rio made in the months that followed.

    Days without Agatha - without kissing her, fucking her, tangling into her - scattered forward like loose papers in the wind. The rhythm of Rio's life disintegrated without that force to push against, flirt with, resist.

    So - almost without realizing it - she did the only thing that made sense: she made trouble. Picked fights. Sabotaged small things just to get under the Reaper’s skin. Because even conflict was better than absence. She had entered a new kamikaze era.

    After the abrupt end of their after-hours activities the production of Lady Death blurred into watercolor left out in the rain. Monday bled into Tuesday. Thursday bled into Sunday. The days became indistinguishable, reduced to labels without substance.

    Only Agatha’s intrusions cut through: edits, calls, casting discussions - each one salt rubbed into an open wound.

    And Rio hated herself. Not Agatha - herself. For catching feelings in a minefield. For planting tenderness in hostile ground. For mistaking a biohazard of a heart for a safe house. For missing her.

    And it wasn’t just the sex. That would’ve been simpler.

    No.

    She missed Agatha’s small, devastating attentions: The way she pulled her close mid-conversation.

    The goddamn chivalry - because Agatha, infuriatingly, was a gentleman through and through. The secret shimmer in those sky-blue eyes as she went down on her, hunger dissolving into delicacy.

    The way she cupped her face before every kiss, grounding her, disarming her. The absentminded hand stroking her hair and tracing her spine while scrolling emails. She missed the morning ritual - Mornin’, sweetheart. Sleep well? - asked every day as if the answer mattered.

    She missed brushing her teeth only to feel Agatha’s arms wrap around her waist, lips pressing into her cheek while their eyes met in the mirror.

    The ridiculous gallantry of the car door opened for her every morning - even if followed by the secrecy of being dropped two streets away so no one saw them arrive together. The long, unhurried kiss before Agatha sent her off with a playful smack and that whispered benediction: Go get them, tiger.

    She missed the laughter. The playful tickles mid-argument. The illusion of safety - the fake safehouse Agatha had built with her good manners and steady hands.

    And she loathed herself for believing in it - and worse, for wanting it back, knowing it was counterfeit.

    Sometimes the anger burned so hot it scorched her imagination. She fantasized about burning it all down - because torching Agatha’s car hadn’t been enough. She wanted to raze every cursed place Agatha had ever touched her.

    By now, Rio knew the truth: patience, composure, calm - all the grace she’d forced on herself these past months - hadn’t bought her a damn thing with her favorite disaster of a woman. None of it mattered. All she’d gotten was being bitten, over and over again, by that wild, glorious, feral creature.

    And once that card had been played, there was no going back. Rio no longer knew how to ask for what she wanted without it becoming open war. A direct affront. The only language Agatha seemed to understand was savagery - and Rio was more than ready to answer in kind. The only reason she hadn’t unleashed it yet - the only thing keeping her claws sheathed - was Darcy. That piece still had to fall into place. But the moment Darcy’s seat at the table was secured? The second that box was ticked and Rio was free to move without collateral - then? Hell was gonna break loose.

    That was the plan.

    So for an entire fucking month she kept circling a new pattern: push, test, retreat. Because what went on between Rio Vidal and Agatha Harkness in the new writers’ room - and everywhere else - had nothing to do with scripts. It was survival. Seduction. Provocation. A choreography of destruction played out under fluorescent lights.

    They weren’t editing pages or negotiating budgets; they were dismantling each other with the elegance of fencers trading blows, the patience of jewel thieves, and the cold accuracy of snipers. Notes arrived like flirtation. Feedback landed like foreplay. Every suggestion scrawled in blood-red ink carried a sting; every cut was a hidden caress. Scripts bled. Egos flared. Desire hummed steady beneath it all.

    To outsiders, the dynamic looked toxic, maybe even reportable. To them, it was fluency. Trouble was their shared tongue. Every meeting teetered between open war and the heat of hate sex waiting to ignite. Every draft was a skirmish doubling as invitation. Every memo, a performance of power disguised as professionalism. They made each other’s work lives just difficult enough to feel personal. Collaboration felt less like creativity and more like trench warfare.

    Lady Death limped forward like a wounded animal under Rio’s kamikaze style of leading. The new showrunner drifted into conference rooms with eyes like locked doors. Her tug-of- war with the Reaper was already legend - reckless, fearless, detached even from her own dream project.

    Rio wanted a reaction. She craved it. And yet she was grateful for the buffer of colleagues, whiteboards scribbled to exhaustion, smoke breaks, endless fake coffee runs. Because she wasn’t sure she could survive being trapped alone in a room with Agatha again. When people asked what was wrong, she called it creative block. Which was true the way a barricade is just inconvenient. It wasn’t a block, it was a siege. A protest. Every missed deadline another thread yanked from Agatha’s tapestry.

    Most days, she rationed her words to clipped syllables: - Do whatever you want.

    - Not my problem.

    - Talk to someone else.

    Then she’d pivot away, always away - as if acknowledging Agatha was reluctant charity. And yet, she kept showing up. Day after day, walking back into the fire. Hooked. Haunted. Because what kept her awake at night wasn’t what Agatha had done - but what she hadn’t. She hadn’t fired her.

    Not even after the car.

    * For God’s sake. She had torched Agatha Fucking Harkness’s Aston Martin. In broad daylight. In the executive parking lot. And...nothing happened! *

    Agatha did nothing. Nobody did anything. No reprimand. No HR ambush. No memo, no lawsuit, not even a whisper.

    It was a relief, yes, but also strangely disappointing.

    Rio waited for the fallout: She braced herself for the venomous 3 a.m. Voicemail, the ambush in a boardroom, the quiet meeting where her badge would be deactivated by security, her name erased from every call sheet.

    But nothing ever came.

    No reaction. No punishment. No rage.

    Just silence.

    For now, Agatha even seemed almost…playful. She smiled whenever Rio ignored her.

    Another month bled away in avoidance and anger.

    Rio ducked emails, laughed at executives, drifted through meetings half-drunk or high. Her reputation spread: Difficult. Impossible. Toxic.

    And still - the hammer never fell. Agatha didn’t storm in. Didn’t call her out. Didn’t even raise her voice. She retreated instead into sterile professionalism. Emails only. Silence sharp enough to be its own weapon.

    And for Rio - who only ever wanted more from her - that silence was the cruelest cut. So her guerrilla war dragged on.

    Until eventually, over something as stupid as a broken AC, she cracked. The day of a crucial script delivery - one she had no intention of handing in. The AC failure started small, a warm drift. Then the air thickened. Shirts clung. Patience snapped. Excuses to work from home multiplied. Sweat pooled, tempers flared, Rio presided like a general over chaos.

    Maintenance had no explanation.

    Rio didn’t need one. She could smell Agatha’s fingerprints - meticulous, deniable, almost admirable.

    And she wasn’t entirely wrong.

    The truth was, they weren’t even looking at the same picture anymore.

    What Rio kept mistaking for a toxic defense of her pride was, in the Head Producer’s eyes, quickly becoming a liability that needed fixing. Where Rio saw duels of sabotage, Agatha - calculating now- saw pragmatic calls that had to be made, fast, if they wanted the multimillion-dollar machine to keep running.

    Calls Rio, as showrunner, should have been making but wasn’t. Calls that, left unanswered, would drag them both under.

    That stubborn, insubordinate oddball wasn’t built for that kind of pragmatism. Not yet. Agatha knew it. She’d been indulging her - but she wasn’t wrong. The job was already eating Rio alive.

    Too much confidence tangled with too much doubt. Fire and ice. Bravado and breakdown. The contradictions had been tearing at her for weeks. Sleepless nights, nicotine shakes, THC haze, way too much Red Bull - she was unraveling, and fast.

    She needed to be alone. Right now.

    High, needy, broken, fraying at the edges, she waved the team off and slipped toward the terrace behind the old gym. A forgotten scrap of altitude where the air was thinner, cleaner - where, for just a moment, she could breathe above the city’s metallic grind. What she didn’t know was that the hammer she’d been dreading was about to fall, but not the way she expected. Agatha Harkness had built her career on wrangling impossible artists into successful shows. And one of her keenest skills as a producer was knowing the difference between when to bring the hammer down… and when to build with it.

    The door, as always, was – supposedly - padlocked.

    A laminated sign warned: CLOSED FOR RENOVATION UNTIL FURTHER NOTICE.

    Which was laughable. Rio had smoked here nearly every day since joining Westview. The terrace was in perfect condition - just forgotten.

    She checked the corridor. Empty. And knelt by the lock. Two twists, a soft click. She was outside.

    Sunlight struck her full in the face.

    And there - already waiting, already sovereign, framed by the blazing sky as though she’d orchestrated the entire scene - sat the most infuriating creature on the planet. Agatha Harkness sat at the far edge of the terrace like it belonged to her. One leg crossed over the other, oversized tortoiseshell glasses slicing her face into elegant geometry. A cigarette balanced between two fingers, her hair spilling loose over her shoulders, each strand catching fire in the sun.

    She didn’t just sit. She presided.

    The city below wasn’t her backdrop - it was her stage.

    The terrace might as well have been renamed, redrawn on city maps as Harkness Heights. “You’re late” she said.

    Rio froze in the doorway, her pulse rattling in her throat. She glanced at her phone. Half past one. Of course. Agatha had planned this. Timed the AC fiasco perfectly to line up with her lunch break, knowing Rio would run here. Predicting her, like she always did. * Damn her. *

    “So now you’ve staked out the terrace too?” Rio asked.

    She leaned against the wall, aiming for casual, but her body betrayed her - strung tight. They’d made out here more times than she could count, always at lunch, always rushed, half- drunk on nicotine, adrenaline, and want. The city below, a shameless voyeur. Of course she’d claim this spot eventually. Every corner Rio touched, this gorgeous nightmare marked as hers.

    Agatha didn’t even turn her head. She inhaled slowly, lips closing around the filter, then exhaled toward the sun. Smoke curled upward, dissolving into heat like it had nowhere better to be.

    “Oh, darling,” she said at last, her voice languid, almost sweet, though edged with fatigue. “this terrace was mine long before you ever set foot in this building.” Only then did she tilt her head - just enough for her troublesome delight to catch the faint curl of her lips.

    “You can stay. I don’t mind sharing” Agatha added, sliding her glasses up onto her head. The movement tamed her wild hair into something like an accidental crown, making her already unbearable beauty sharpen into something imperious. “Especially now that you remember how to talk to me”

    It felt like a ambush. It always did with her.

    Agatha arched one brow, patient as a cat, waiting for the little mouse to twitch. Rio’s fingers fumbled with the unlit joint in her hand, suddenly ridiculous. She’d come out here to breathe, to escape. Instead, she’d walked straight into the storm she’d been avoiding for the past two months. Weed had always been her refuge, but against Agatha it was as useless as a paper shield in a gunfight.

    “Stay. We need to talk” the producer said firmly.

    Her tone was calm but coaxing, threaded with that quiet command Rio knew too well. The same voice she’d once used to devastating effect in bed - the one that never sounded like a request, and yet always got its way.

    Rio angled her body toward the door, clinging to the safety of avoidance. Better to be a confrontational coward than let her guard slip. Safer for her sanity.

    “I don’t care what a liar like you have to say.”

    “You’re still coming at me with that?” Agatha tipped her head back, letting out a bitter sigh as she exhaled smoke into the pitiless sky. “Drop the pity act”

    The sunlight made her eyes look almost cruel in their brightness.

    “I need you focused. I need your head in this project.”

    Her subordinate barked a laugh, incredulous. “You mean obedient.”

    Agatha didn’t bother to deny it.

    Her eyes darkened, sharpening into something hungry. For one charged beat, the image of her sweet delirium - naked, pliant, waiting - flashed hot and uninvited across her mind. “God, don’t tempt me”

    The slip was dangerous, indulgent, and she caught herself with a sigh, like yanking hard on her own leash.

    “But at work? Focused will do.”

    The shift in power was unmistakable. In that instant, she wasn’t Rio’s ex-lover. She was the Head Producer, immovable, calculating, in absolute control.

    The truth was, Agatha wasn’t here to toy with her. She was changing tactics. She knew pressing too hard would only push Rio deeper into sabotage—not just of them, but of the production itself. And that was something neither of them could afford. “You want me all in on a project I wish I’d never let fall into your filthy hands?” Her tone was cool, but the bite in it was unmistakable. “You serious?”

    “Dead serious.” Agatha didn’t blink. Sunlight flashed across the lenses perched in her hair, underlining every syllable.

    Stepping up to the railing, Rio snapped.

    “You’re the worst boss I’ve ever had.”

    She knew it was a lie, but the words still landed like shrapnel.

    Her perfect mistake didn’t flinch. She wore her armor well - the ruthless, soulless boss. But Rio knew better. Knew that beneath the ice, Agatha cared. About the work. About the crew. About keeping the machine alive. Beneath all that cynicism, her ruthlessness carried its own ethic. Not spotless. Not pure. But effective. Efficient.

    The kind of ethic that made bitter men mutter she’d climbed on looks alone, when in truth she was the sharpest mind in any room she walked into.

    She dared to do what others wouldn’t - throw herself into the fire for the sake of a project she believed in. Not out of recklessness, but conviction. She pushed against the edges of what television was supposed to be, bending rules until they snapped, chasing something truer, better, more alive. She wanted shows that didn’t just entertain. That didn’t just fill an hour, but left a mark.

    Rio hated her for a thousand personal reasons. But even with all her flaws, she couldn’t help but respect her as a superior.

    The smell of the cigarette drifted between them, warm, invasive, the exact temperature of her attention.

    “Aren’t you tired of picking fights with me?” that gorgeous strategist asked softly. “This little rebel act is only making things worse.”

    “Don’t know what you expect me to say.”

    Agatha tilted her head, pretending to think, her mouth curving into a mock-thoughtful smile. “Hmm. How about, ‘I’ll quit this self-destructive stunt’?”

    Her favorite troublemaker turned to face her fully, eyes locking on hers, voice steady and defiant.

    “Do you really think I’m afraid of you?”

    “Of course not” Agatha’s answer was instant, smooth, unapologetic. “You wouldn’t be half as interesting if you were”

    The silence that followed wasn’t empty - it thrummed, tight as a bowstring. Agatha rose from the low stone wall where she’d been perched, every movement measured - gravity itself seemed to bend around her. She didn’t just stand. She claimed. The terrace. The skyline. The shimmering heat of the afternoon. All of it bent, subtly, to her will. She drew deep on her cigarette, holding the smoke as if savoring a secret, then released a crown of silver that curled into the burning sky.

    And Rio - furious, restless, helplessly enthralled - stood frozen.

    * Shit. Why was this woman so...magnificent? *

    “I still want to bet on your talent” Agatha said at last. Her tone was steady, almost soft, which only made the words cut deeper. “But if you keep throwing it away just because I didn’t give you what you wanted… I can’t protect you from yourself.”

    She hadn’t raised her voice. She didn’t need to. The words were cold, brutal, the cleanest dissection of Rio’s recent recklessness.

    Her defiant pet turned halfway toward her, eyes feral. “Don’t flatter yourself.” "Too late"

    Her most perilous secret smiled. That smile. Mischief, risk, temptation. A crossroads-demon smile that promised either a kiss or a knife to the heart. She kept it intact as her gaze slid toward the golden sprawl of Los Angeles below.

    Suddenly, she closed the distance, stepping up to the railing until she stood shoulder to shoulder with Rio. The heat of her cigarette drifted between them, invasive. The wind tossed dark strands of her hair across her cheek, and a few brushed against Rio’s face like an accidental touch neither of them acknowledged.

    The silence hummed, thick with possibilities: a kiss, a slap, a confession, an ending. “I don’t pay you to screw with my job” Agatha said at last, her voice low and measured as she turned to face her tense subordinate. “You’ve got a show to run.”

    Smoke curled from her lips as she exhaled, straight toward Rio. Intimate. Territorial. And when her gaze dipped, uninvited, to Rio’s mouth, it scorched like a brand. Rio’s chest tightened. She hated herself for noticing, for pressing her tongue to the inside of her cheek, dragging it slowly up and down, grinning as if on reflex. For letting that lustful look slam into her like home, no matter how much she wished it didn’t “So do me a favor” the producer went on, her eyes still fixed on her employee’s mouth. “Change your strategy. You’re too damn good to waste it all on a vendetta.” A pause.

    “And so is your friend.”

    It was meant as recognition. A reminder of what Rio was capable of, what she could still salvage. But it landed like a threat.

    The writer's breath caught. Disbelief twisted her lips into a smile with no warmth at all. “Such a petty, sadistic little cu..”

    “Careful” The Head Producer cut in smoothly - not unkind, but with enough steel to remind her who she was talking to, who held the cards. She flicked the last of her ash lazily over the railing, toward the building below - her empire, Westview Productions. For weeks she’d allowed Rio her rebellion, her malicious compliance. But the line was near now. Too near. She couldn’t indulge her forever - not with a son at home counting on her paycheck, not with millions at stake. Once, she might have played the long game, leaning on her instincts, certain the storm would break in her favor because it always had. But that was before Nicky. Before she began dismantling the woman she used to be to rebuild herself into something even harder, steadier. Unshakable. And more reliable.

    If this beautiful menace couldn’t come to her senses - if she insisted on clinging to her rage - Agatha would have no choice but to leave her behind. Professionally speaking. The wounded showrunner regretted not lighting the joint earlier. Now her hands were free and itching to grab Agatha by the throat and shove her clean off the terrace. No one else alive could shred her composure faster.

    “This is all your fault” she spat. The words erupted as if they’d been caged in her chest for weeks, clawing their way free.

    “True.”

    “And?”

    Agatha shrugged. She’d never bet on a losing dog. She was the one who put them down. Rio needed to understand: Agatha didn’t want to destroy her, but if Lady Death crumbled, she wouldn’t hesitate to make her the scapegoat. Better one body buried than both. "Just tell me you heard me" she said finally. Her eyes locked on Rio’s with an intensity that pressed too close to something else, something Rio had refused to acknowledge since that office fight. "Tell me you got it "

    Caught off guard by the weight of that stare, she answered tightly: "I heard you, boss. Loud and clear."

    They stood side by side, both staring out at the endless sprawl of the city. The world below moved on - traffic, voices, life. But up here, the terrace was its own orbit, circling only the two of them.

    “Is it worth it? All of this?” Rio finally asked, her voice low, trembling with too many layers - resentment, desire, grief, defiance. It was the kind of line loaded with subtext, the sort that belonged in a script - too perfect, really, to waste on real life.

    The exec let the silence stretch. That was her way - never rushing, never surrendering tempo. Even when indulging herself, she never lost sight of the bigger pìcture. “We’ll see” was all she answered.

    Both women sighed at the same time, their breaths rising and falling like two tides colliding on the same shore.

    Rio’s gaze dropped to the unlit joint still clenched between her fingers. She turned it over once, like maybe the answer to everything was scribbled somewhere along its thin paper seam.

    Agatha followed the look. With a flick of her wrist, she pulled out a lighter and held it up between them.

    “May I?”

    Rio hesitated, but she slid the joint between her lips and leaned in. Sparks jumped as Agatha rolled the wheel, the flame refusing to catch.

    In a low, teasing murmur, that beautiful psychopath whispered “Off the record...if you ever feel like unpacking what happened between us...”

    The wheel struck again. This time the lighter caught, flaring bright, throwing light across the veins of her long, witchlike hand.

    “...I know a Thai place worth dying for.”

    Her hypnotic blue eyes glinted, locked on Rio’s dark ones.

    But the tension was so sharp it snapped.

    “I hate you” Rio muttered around the joint, raw, overwhelmed. “I hate this.” She stepped back too fast, and flicked the joint off the terrace with all the force of her frustration, watching it tumble toward the street below.

    Agatha shut the lighter with a clean click, her face perfectly calm, not giving away even a flicker of offense.

    “Or I can keep my distance. That works too” she said evenly. “Your call.” Rio stared at her, words rattling around in her chest, refusing to settle. * What did she really want from this vicious enchantress? How did she want this curse between them to unfold? *

    Agatha, unexpectedly tender, laid one perfect hand over hers where it gripped the railing. “Hey. For now, let’s just focus on the job. Okay?” she said softly.

    Rio exhaled like she was giving up a piece of herself, and nodded. She didn’t trust the heat crawling under her skin. She didn’t trust this perfect woman. She didn’t trust herself - least of all when she was trapped alone with temptation incarnate.

    As if reading her mind, that mesmerizing devious goddess closed the space between them. One step, and suddenly she was right there - so close their breaths tangled. Smoke curled from her lips, and Rio took it in despite herself, the bitter taste clinging to her tongue. Without warning, Agatha slipped her hand into Rio’s pocket. Her touch lingered, fingertips brushing against the showrunner’s thigh.

    Instinct snapped through Rio: her free hand shot to that reckless maniac’s hip, meant to shove her away. Instead, it just… stayed there. Like her body had already made the choice her mind refused to admit.

    The merciless seductress smirked, knowing, daring. She left the lighter in Rio’s pocket before drawing her hand back with unhurried grace.

    “Keep it” she murmured. “Something tells me you’re in need of a fresh one.” The line - a clear jab at what Rio had done to her car - hung there, provocation disguised as generosity.

    Panic flared. With a sharp yank, Rio tore her trapped hand free from under Agatha’s and shoved herself back.

    She spun on her heel and strode for the door, hips swaying in that maddening walk that still drove her ex-lover insane.

    Agatha stayed behind. She didn’t chase. She didn’t need to. She knew she’d struck a nerve - that Rio, despite everything, had listened.

    Leaning back against the railing, her lips curved in a private smile. She replayed the exchange, tallying it up like a gambler reading cards. A handful of words. A flicker of touch. A reaction she hadn’t earned in weeks.

    She hadn’t coaxed even one of those tiny little stutters out of her delicious bad girl, but time would take care of that. They’d get there.

    “Not bad” she murmured to the empty air, flicking the spent filter over the edge and watching it vanish into the street below.

    The needle had shifted. Just a fraction - but in her favor.

    She’d thought that lunch break on the terrace would be the lowest point. Awkward, humiliating, buried and done with. The kind of memory you shove into a locked drawer and promise yourself never to touch again.

    Looking back, Rio realized she had been naïve.

    The real violation didn’t come as a reprimand exhaled in smoke or a hand pressing where it shouldn’t.

    No.

    The worst came dressed as strategy. As an asset to the series. As help. Agatha played it perfectly. She wielded the reach of her position, crossing a line so fine it made Rio want to scream. Which, if you asked Agatha, counted as progress. She’d been starving for a reaction - any reaction - from the screenwriter who had promised, after the terrace incident, to behave.

    And Rio had behaved. Technically. But not in the way Agatha wanted. Not in the way that mattered. At best, she was giving half of what she was capable of. At worst, she was twisting orders, bending them out of shape, turning compliance into a kind of sabotage. It was better than outright rebellion, yes - but only barely.

    Agatha let her. For a while. She gave Rio rope, pretended at patience, allowed her the illusion of freedom. But the executive had eyes, and what she saw was simple: Rio was drowning. Not from lack of talent - she had talent in excess, more than most people could dream of - but because she refused to let herself be taught. Refused to accept her help. That, the producer decided, could not stand. So she did what she always did. She took control.

    The move was brutal, and timed with cruelty: the handoff from pre-production into production.

    Directors, editors, designers - every critical hire passed through Agatha’s desk, not Rio's. All of them brilliant, seasoned, award-winning. And loyal. But not to the woman whose name sat on the contracts. Their loyalty belonged to the woman who had chosen them. Rio felt the shift instantly. On paper, she was still showrunner. In practice, her authority had been gutted before she’d even sat in the chair. Legally, she couldn’t undo a thing without detonating clauses that would bankrupt them before the first frame was shot. So she did what she had to: swallowed the insult, ran the meetings, smiled through clenched teeth while everyone in the room listened for Agatha’s voice instead of hers. She told herself she didn’t care. But the truth pressed against her like a bruise. And then Agatha pushed further.

    The coup de grâce came dressed as a support system. A watchdog disguised as guidance. A safeguard nobody had asked for.

    Agatha had imagined it differently. In her head, Rio would be beside her - guided, tethered, dependent. She would learn with Agatha’s hand steadying hers. But Rio had refused, flat and stubborn. She’d insisted she could handle the work alone. And to her credit, she was learning - brilliant in flashes, fumbling in others, clawing her way into the rare air of the showrunner’s chair, where a single misstep could kill you.

    Lately, she’d even begun to adapt. Fighting less. Owning pieces of the role. Maybe even enjoying them, despite the endless battle lines between her and Agatha. But it wasn’t enough.

    If Rio wouldn’t take her hand, then she’d weave a net around her instead. Invisible. Inescapable.

    That net arrived in the form of an old ally: a veteran consulting showrunner, flown in from a New York partner company. Not officially Westview, but close enough to slip through the door without resistance. Someone with gravitas. Steady hands. A résumé that could silence a room. A profesional Agatha trusted to keep her reluctant protégé from burning herself to ash. Rio discovered the setup the day she came back from a production meeting, herbal tea in hand, expecting the sanctuary of her brand-new office to be empty. She opened the door...and froze.

    Her haven was already claimed.

    Agatha sat in her chair as if she’d been born to it, one leg elegantly crossed, perfectly at ease. Her posture radiated ownership; it declared that the chair, the office, the entire world belonged to her. It was Rio who felt like the intruder.

    And leaning against the desk beside her, as if the furniture had been designed to complement her presence, was a woman Rio had never seen before.

    Dark hair, warmer than Agatha’s. Mid-forties. Skin that seemed immune to bad lighting. Bold glasses framing brown eyes alive with both wit and authority. Her clothes carried that effortless-expensive air - sleek, tailored, modern. Her jacket fell open like an invitation. They weren’t identical, but together they rhymed. Variations on a theme. Two women who knew exactly what weight they carried when they walked into a room.

    And they were laughing.

    Not the brittle, polite laughter of corporate courtesies, but something warmer. Intimate. The kind of laughter that leaned in close, that brushed fingertips without noticing, that hinted at old jokes and older trust.

    The stranger’s hand rested on Agatha’s shoulder, fingers curving there with a familiarity that should’ve taken years to earn. She leaned in, voice pitched low.

    “You’re impossible, Aggie. Always dragging me into trouble.”

    Rio’s stomach dropped.

    * Aggie. That nickname again. A name from a private world beyond these walls. A world she’d never been let into. *

    Her own voice came out sharper, cooler than she felt.

    “The hell’s going on here?”

    The stranger turned slowly, her hand still anchored on Agatha’s shoulder. Her smile was lazy, confident.

    “Just vibes” she said, like that explained everything.

    Agatha cleared her throat, slipping into that professional smile that looked harmless until it cut. She rose from Rio’s chair like she was returning something she hadn’t borrowed. “Vidal,” she said smoothly, “let me introduce you. This is Maybelline Parker. She’ll be consulting on Lady Death, here to support you with whatever you need for the series.” “Support me?”

    Agatha let Rio's words hang just long enough before adding “She’s one of the most respected communications experts in the industry. You’re very lucky to have her. She’s in high demand.” That last line wasn’t aimed at Rio. It was aimed sideways, at May. And the glance that came with it carried an intimacy that should’ve been private.

    Maybelline pushed off the desk with feline ease, her hand brushing down the Head Producer's arm before giving it a squeeze. She laughed softly, affection laced with mockery. “Oh, Aggie. You always oversell.”

    * Aggie. Again. Did everyone outside the office call her that, or what? * Her gaze slid to Rio, taking her in with one cool sweep. Clinical. Curious. Unlike Agatha’s usual professionl tight smile, hers was easy, disarming.

    “Nice to finally meet you. Your boss here hasn’t stopped singing your praises” she said, tipping her head toward the producer.

    She extended her hand. “Please, call me May.”

    “Ugh, don’t call her that” Agatha cut in, her tone smooth, corrective. “Maybelline is so much more beautiful.”

    Agent Melinda May lingered in her mind like an echo. She much prefered keep calling her friend Maybelline.

    The correction landed heavy.

    Consultant-May only chuckled, unbothered. “She’ll call me whatever I want her to, Agatha.” Her eyes never left Rio’s.

    “Doesn’t it drive you crazy? How bossy she gets? She can’t help it. It’s that L.A. killer instinct ”

    Rio expected Agatha’s usual blade of a comeback, the kind that left people gutted. But Agatha only rolled her eyes. A strange, almost indulgent response.

    * Interesting *

    Most people folded around Agatha, flustered, eager to please, cowed. But not this woman. This woman with her easy laugh matched her. Rio hadn’t seen that before. Not from anyone but herself.

    Her mouth betrayed her, curving against her will. “I already like you.” May took her hand. She didn’t just shake it, she covered it with her other palm, holding on a breath too long. Her voice dropped, low and teasing.

    “Great” she said, eyes locked on her. “'Cause I fully intend for us to be good friends” “How is that even possible when you’re here to babysit me?” Rio’s voice came out brittle. May flicked Agatha a glance - a loaded look, full of something Rio didn’t have a name for, but recognized instantly as trouble.

    The Head Producer cut in before the new consultant could speak. “Think of it as mentorship” she clarified crisply.

    The delivery of her next line was too polished, almost rehearsed: “Running a show isn’t just scripts and writers’ rooms. It’s budgets, schedules, casting, post- production, corporate politics, press campaigns, damage control. Westview wants to protect their investment. When we take a chance on fresh talent, we pair them with someone...” “..Seasoned” May finished, smoothly slotting herself into the rhythm.

    The two women shared another glance, rich with history.

    “This is a high-budget series” Agatha pressed on, undeterred. “We can’t afford mistakes. Parker is here to make sure there aren’t any.” Rio’s voice was dry, cutting into their shared harmony. “So, an expensive babysitter” May tilted her head, watching Rio with an amused, intrigued expression. Like a scientist who had just discovered a new species and couldn’t wait to see what it did under pressure. “Well, I’ll leave you two to it.” Agatha said while smoothing her jacket and moving toward the door, her hand grazing the desk as though sealing some private pact. “We’ll finish catching up later” she added, her voice softened, not quite tender, but close enough to pass.

    She tilted her head slightly and tapped her cheek with one finger, a wordless invitation. To Rio’s surprise, May leaned in without hesitation, brushing a light kiss against Agatha’s cheek. Agatha answered with a wink, casual as breathing, as if giving the Reaper a little peck on the face were the most natural thing in the world.

    * Oh, so Agatha and May were just friends *

    Not lovers. Not ex-lovers. Not even strictly colleagues. Friends.

    But then again, Rio couldn’t be sure. With Agatha, lines blurred until they dissolved. And both women carried a flirtatious charge so naturally it was impossible to tell where performance ended and intimacy began. Trying to read them was like trying to hold smoke. And that’s when the truth hit Rio, ugly, undeniable. She didn’t actually know a damn thing about Agatha. Not what her friendships looked like. Not who she trusted, or why. If she hadn’t been so consumed by the mystery, she might have recognized the gesture for what it was: proof. Proof that maybe - just maybe - Agatha was trying. Not only to mend their fractured working dynamic, but to let Rio see a little more of the woman beneath the armor.

    But pain had narrowed Rio’s vision until she couldn’t see past it. Instead of reading May’s presence for what it truly was: Agatha lowering her guard by bringing someone she trusted, an olive branch disguised as strategy. Rio saw only provocation. A problem. At the threshold, Agatha turned back.

    She wanted nothing more than to let Rio know she hadn’t stopped thinking about her. To kiss her until that infuriating, irresistible girl finally understood just how much she missed her: in her bed, in her life.

    But Rio hated her. Or so she claimed.

    And Maybelline was standing right there.

    And business was business.

    So she lingered a beat too long, held Rio’s gaze, gave the slightest nod, and said curtly, “Vidal” before slipping out without waiting for an answer.

    It wasn’t retreat. It was strategy. Staying would have poisoned whatever fragile trust might be forming between May and Rio. May was nearly her equal in the producing game, and charismatic enough to win Rio over on her own. Agatha knew it. She needed it. If those two clicked, Lady Death would run like clockwork. If they didn’t… the whole series could collapse under its own weight.

    The door clicked shut behind her. And somehow the room felt heavier, not lighter, as if Agatha had left a silent claim hanging in the air. On Rio. On the project. On everything. The showrunner let the silence stretch, curiosity chewing at her until she couldn’t resist anymore. She found a way to frame the question that had been eating at her with something that almost passed for casual.

    “So… how does one become friends with the Reaper?”

    May’s mouth curved in the faintest smirk. Her shoulders lifted in an elegant shrug. “We tolerate each other surprisingly well, don't we?”

    That was not at all the kind of answer Rio had expected. Her brow arched, and she let the pause breathe, suspicion and intrigue winding tighter with every second. She could tell there was more.

    May’s lips slanted, sly and knowing.

    “Let’s just say, out of all the assholes in Westview, Aggie’s the one I hate the least. And I like to think the feeling’s mutual.”

    She didn’t stop there.

    “And that brings me to my first piece of advice as your consulting showrunner: there are no friends in this business.”

    Delivered with charm and a honeyed lilt, the answer still landed cold, raw, disarmingly direct. No wonder Agatha liked this woman. They spoke the same language.

    * Mmmkay. So Agatha went and installed her friendlier, debatably crueler, near-double on the project. Terrific *

    May seemed to catch every flicker of doubt passing across Rio’s face. She stepped closer - not invasive, but close enough that her presence warmed the air between them. “Relax” she said lightly. “I’m just here to make sure you shine.”

    Rio’s brow arched, voice flat with irony.

    “You mean keep me in line. And report back to her”

    “Trust me” May replied, tone steady, gaze unblinking. “The Head Producer has better things to do than spy on you.”

    “I can’t think of any” Rio shot back, a quick, cheeky grin tugging at her mouth. That earned a laugh, genuine, unforced.

    “Even if that were true, I’m not here to take control away from you.”

    She leaned against Rio’s desk, crossing her ankles, posture loose but self-assured. “Normally, the rookie steps aside until the veteran decides they’re ready.” she tapped her chest “That’s how this business usually works. Showrunning isn’t just stressful; it’s brutal. Corporations eat first-timers alive. You’re gonna have to be exceptional if you even pretend to survive this job.”

    Rio bristled, pulse quickening. No matter how warm May’s voice sounded, she was still Agatha’s ally. And anyone in Agatha’s orbit was suspect.

    “Wow, that was awfully close to a pep talk” she said dryly, dropping her backpack onto the desk with a thud. “With all due respect, I don’t need one.”

    The consultant's smile widened, not wolfish like Agatha’s, but warm, playful, with a steadiness that disarmed rather than threatened.

    “With all due respect” she countered, studying Rio with a frankness that stripped the teasing from her tone. “I don’t give a damn what you think you need.”

    When she spoke again, her voice had edged with curiosity, a hunger looking for a crack to slip through.

    “She says your special. I can’t wait to see what it is she sees in you.” Rio blinked, caught off guard. A dry laugh broke out before she could stop it. “Right. The Reaper thinks I’m special. Sure.”

    The words had bite, but the hit landed lower than she wanted to admit. Praise from Agatha - professional or otherwise - had become so rare... And she was still a sucker for it. May studied her face a moment too long before looking away, as though she’d brushed up against something private. She let it go without a word, slipping back into the current of conversation.

    “That’s why I’m here” she said simply. “Curiosity got the better of me. Had to see the Reaper’s secret weapon with my own eyes.”

    “I’m not her secret anything” Rio shot back, the defense automatic.

    The woman who moved and spoke like Agatha but wasn’t her at all smirked.

    “Okay, I’ll bite.” Her tone was light, but her eyes stayed razor-focused. “Let’s call out what’s obvious.”

    She lifted a hand and ticked points off on her fingers, one by one.

    “You’re young. You’re talented. You’re gorgeous. Still mostly under the radar. And somehow, you walked off with one of the biggest deals of the year like it was easy. Babe, you’re clearly Westview’s new bet. The Reaper’s golden gamble.”

    Rio frowned, confusion crossing her face before she could mask it.

    “Oh my God” May breathed, grinning wider. “You really had no idea.”

    The mischief in her smile turned into something darker. Her gaze swept over Rio, slow and deliberate, before curling back into provocation.

    “You’re way too cute to be this clueless.”

    The tease, landed heavier than expected - half playful, half sincere - and it unsettled Rio more than she wanted to admit.

    * Was she imagining it? Or was Agatha’s disarmingly attractive friend actually flirting with her? *

    May’s smile turned sly.

    “I can’t wait for you to surprise me”

    * Yep. That was exactly what was happening. *

    She wasn’t Agatha, but she had the same mercurial pull, the same quicksilver way of turning a moment. Not just attractive. Not just charming. That spark - volatile, magnetic - tugged at Rio whether she liked it or not.

    If May wanted to flirt? Fine. Rio could flirt right back. And what better way to remind her infuriating ex-owner that she’d already lost than to take this little poisoned gift and twist it into something of her own?

    She leaned in, lips curving.

    “How about lunch?” she offered, her voice smooth. “I’ll catch you up on the project…and you can tell me more about yourself while we’re at it.”

    That did it.

    May’s grin widened even more - open on the surface, wicked underneath - as she shifted just enough to hold the door for her.

    “Now that sounds like my idea of fun.”

    Two weeks later, after what the Head Producer no doubt thought was some grand act of mercy, Rio finally stopped getting the whispered threats about her job and the digs at her work ethic.

    Apparently, all it had taken were a few half-assed steps in the “right” direction, nudged, if you could even call it that, by the shiny new consultant who’d somehow made herself indispensable overnight.

    Naturally, that didn’t mean Darcy got promoted to co–showrunner.

    HR’s stance was carved in stone: Westview only ever hired one showrunner per series. A rule The Wicked Reaper herself had recently installed, obviously.

    So instead, Rio’s co-creator got a title that looked fancy on paper - half managerial, half creative - but in practice was pure window dressing. One step below the throne: close enough to watch every decision, never close enough to make one.

    And yet, in her boundless optimism, that sweet woman never complained. She probably didn’t even notice. She’d taken the job with the same wide-eyed glee she brought to everything: thrilled Lady Death was finally happening, thrilled her name would be in the credits, thrilled Westview had actually let her in.

    Her socials made it obvious. Behind-the-scenes selfies with Rio. Grainy clips of the crew cracking up during table reads. Coffee-stained script pages, marker-scribbled whiteboards. Sometimes even flirty little videos with pre-production staff, blushing, shameless, pure Darcy.

    And Rio? Privately, she blamed the Head Producer for draining every ounce of joy from what should’ve been the highlight of her career. For turning creation into labor. For poisoning pride with duty. In every candid Darcy posted, Rio looked like a hostage - shoulders tight, jaw locked, expression hovering somewhere between deadpan and detonation. Not joy. Compliance.

    The only reason she was in them at all was because the boss had made it a requirement: online and physical proof of collaboration and creative flow.

    And as if that weren’t enough, Agatha went further. Under the pretense of “supporting the production,” she didn’t just follow the official Lady Death account.

    She followed Darcy’s.

    And Rio’s.

    Rio only found out after her last round of notes came back with one particularly infuriating line about the Fugitive Killer: She should be more than a victim. Make her powerful, complex, not just a love interest.

    Insulting, in its implication. Because Agatha knew – knew - Rio would never reduce a woman to just a love interest. That note wasn’t feedback, it was a provocation. A jab dressed up as encouragement.

    So Rio took the note. And twisted it.

    In the newest drafts, the Fugitive Killer was no longer a tragic anti-heroine misunderstood by the world. She had evolved into something unhinged: less victim, more charismatic sociopath with a God complex. A woman with no capacity for intimacy, no interest in connection. Ruthless. Manipulative. Treacherous.

    In other words, she wrote Agatha.

    She was still polishing one of those scenes when Darcy burst into her office, grinning like she’d just won an Emmy.

    “That’s it. We’ve made it. Hollywood is ours.” Her bestie declared, breathless with excitement.

    Rio didn’t even look up from her laptop. “Sentences, Darcy. I need full sentences. Preferably with context.”

    Her friend, undeterred, shoved her phone in Rio’s face.

    “The freakin' Reaper just liked our new post. The one of us working from home.” Rio blinked. On the screen, the notification glared back at her: MotherHarkness liked your photo.

    It burned in the back of her throat like acid.

    She couldn’t decide what pissed her off more - that Agatha was following them, or that Darcy actually sounded excited about it.

    “Who cares?” Rio muttered, batting the phone away. “She’s the worst.”

    Darcy, oblivious, laughed it off. To her, the ice-cold shark had been their champion since day one - shaping the script, steering it into existence. Rio’s hostility made no sense except, maybe, as leftover bitterness from that humiliating chapter months ago, when she had been so obviously, pathetically, head-over-heels for their boss. She had always assumed Rio was just sore about being shot down back in the early Westview days. That the Head Producer had been too professional to indulge her.

    Because that was Agatha everywhere: professional, ruthless, untouchable. “You know I’ve got you, right?” her bestie asked softly, sliding onto the arm of Rio’s chair and looping an arm around her shoulders in that clumsy, loyal way she always used when trying to cheer her up. “If you need to throw something my way, I can handle it.” Poor woman. Smiling in the middle of a war zone, oblivious to the crossfire. Still buzzing from the notification, Darcy tapped into Agatha’s profile. “I wonder who else she follows” she mused, thumbs quick on the glass. “Think we’ve got any mutuals? God, I’d die if we had friends in common. That’d be so cursed.” Rio’s shoulders locked tight.

    It had been months since she’d looked. Not since before. Not since those nights when she’d lie awake in the blue glow of her phone, scrolling through Agatha’s carefully curated snapshots of life outside work - always cool, always clever, always stylish, always infuriatingly perfect.

    Back then, she used to imagine herself inside those frames. Fantasized about Agatha’s world bleeding into hers.

    And for a while, it had.

    For a few chaotic, electric, world-ending months, Rio had been inside that frame - even if she never appeared in the actual pictures.

    But after it ended, she’d sworn off that particular brand of self-inflicted torture. No profile- stalking. No late-night doomscrolling. No rereading captions like they held secret clues. She’d been clean.

    Until now.

    Now she had to sit here - silent, tight-lipped, stomach turning - while Darcy scrolled gleefully through a feed filled with Agatha’s face, her voice, her body, her life. It wasn’t even the photos that gutted her. It was the comments.

    The worship.

    Women didn’t speak to Agatha directly. They spoke about her, like she was a myth, a deity, some unreachable fantasy. Third-person idolatry written in pixelated thirst. Even Darcy noticed.

    “Oh, wow. This is… a lot” she whispered. “You queer women are thirsty as hell.” Amused, she read some out loud, scrolling through the parade of longing: “All ten fingers.”

    “Would sell my soul for a single glance.”

    “A tear rolled down my thigh.”

    “Step on my neck, please.”

    “She could run me over with her car and I’d still thank her.”

    “Ruin me, Mother.”

    “The look. The lips. The tits. The hair. Oh God, Oh God, Oh God.”

    Each line scraped across Rio like crooked nails on raw skin.

    And those weren’t even the worst ones.

    Because soon, they found the others.

    Equally thirsty, but more intimate. More unhinged. Clearly written by women who had been there - who knew exactly what Agatha’s mouth, her hands, her body felt like. Women who had been devoured by her and wanted more. Women who had touched and kissed and bitten that perfect ass that could end world hunger.

    “Miss you between my thights.”

    “It’s been months, boo. Call me.”

    “You don’t have to post my name for me to know you’re talking about me.” “I kept that thing you left at my place. You know the one.”

    “Still thinking of you.”

    “When you coming back for more?”

    Different names. Different faces. All clawing for Agatha’s attention in the same breathless tone, like they were the chosen one.

    Like Agatha hadn’t written the rules of this exact game herself - like she wasn’t the dealer, the house, and the goddamn architect.

    Each new comment. Each new flawless woman. Each new swipe, double tap, or flame emoji. Every single one made it harder for Rio to breathe. They weren’t reminders that she’d been just another notch on Agatha’s bedpost - they were reminders she hadn’t even been that. She was a nobody. Another shadow on the wall.

    Darcy, perched beside her with the kind of concentration most people reserved for true crime docs, clicked through their profiles like a gleeful archaeologist unearthing erotic relics. “Wait… does she only date models?” she asked, her voice half awe, half gossip. Rio didn’t answer. Couldn’t.

    One was a curvy redhead with a movie-star smile and tits so photogenic they practically winked at the camera.

    Another, a sultry brunette with a perfect nose and catlike eyes, her entire feed curated like a Vogue editorial spread.

    Darcy gave a low whistle, grinning as she kept scrolling.

    Next came the porcelain-doll type: tiny, pale, with the expensive sadness of a conceptual artist.

    Then a tall, statuesque woman with cropped hair, bone structure sharp enough to cut glass, lush full lips, and the kind of fashion sense that made you want to thank her just for walking into a room.

    And on it went. Agatha’s digital harem felt endless “Yep. Pretty safe to say her type is straight-up bombshells” Darcy said with a smug little nod, like she’d just cracked some impossible code.

    That one landed like a gut punch.

    “Yeah. Apparently” Rio muttered.

    It was true. Brutally, inescapably true. They were all objectively, painfully hot. Darcy scrolled like she was watching fireworks, delighted at every fresh explosion of beauty. “Damn, look at her” she breathed, tapping a profile: a sunlit blonde with beach-waves and bikini shots straight off a billboard. “Seriously, even I’d let her ruin my life.” She cracked up at her own joke, waiting for Rio to laugh. Rio didn’t. Her nails dug crescents into her palms under the desk.

    “Okay, wait. Hold up.” Darcy sat up straighter, excitement sparking in her voice as she opened another profile, eyes going wide. “She’s verified. Like… famous-famous.” On the screen was basically a portrait of a deity: designer gown draped to perfection, champagne glass dangling from one hand, her smile equal parts inviting and terrifyingly polished. A model. An actual, working, cover-shoot model.

    Darcy let out a low whistle.

    “Holy shit. Riri, a bunch of them are. She’s not just pulling bombshells, she’s pulling names. Like… if the Reaper’s little black book ever leaked? Half the internet would implode.” She cracked up, delighted with the scandal of it.

    But Rio’s stomach just kept sinking. Because Darcy was right. This wasn’t a pattern - it was a kingdom. Agatha wasn’t dating women, she was curating them. A living gallery, each one more flawless than the last.

    And Rio? She wasn’t in the gallery. She wasn’t even a footnote.

    Now it was clear in brutal, high-def clarity: she hadn’t been chosen. She’d been tolerated. A detour. A placeholder.

    Her best friend, blissfully oblivious to the battlefield inches away, leaned back with a grin. “You know what this means, right? Technically… we’re, like, two degrees away from half the world’s top influencers.” She wiggled her brows. “I should start networking.” Rio let out a hollow laugh. Safer than silence.

    Darcy didn’t notice the hollowness.

    No.

    Her so-called best friend, currently her worst enemy, in all her clueless straight-girl innocence, went on with genuine confusion: “But why are all you gorgeous women so obsessed with her? I seriously don’t get it.” She asked it like it was a fun riddle, flicking back to Agatha’s main feed as though the answer might be hidden between posts. Like she wasn’t casually poking at Rio’s bruised, barely- healed heart with every tap.

    A beat later, her laugh exploded across the room.

    “Oh shit. You didn't tell me she posted thirst traps.”

    Rio didn’t need to look. She knew exactly what posts Darcy was talking about. The black-and-white shot: Agatha in nothing but a long sweater, thigh-highs, and stilettos, knees pulled up tight against her chest, posed like she’d been lifted straight from an erotic art film.

    The close-up: Agatha staring straight into the lens, lips parted, middle finger raised, tongue curling slow around the tip as though tasting sin itself.

    And the kill shot: full color, full body, full attitude. Agatha draped over the hood of a vintage car, dress riding so high it should’ve come with legal disclaimers, head tossed back in a wicked laugh aimed square at the camera.

    “Damn, she looks like she’s trying to get us all pregnant” Darcy whispered, awestruck. “Good for you, Ms. Harkness”

    She kept scrolling, until she shrieked and smacked Rio’s arm like she’d just dug up buried treasure.

    “Oh my God! You liked this one! You actually did, you filthy little perv!” Before Rio could protest, the phone was shoved in her face. A carousel of studio shots filled the screen: Agatha in a houndstooth suit, vest buttoned snug, tie loose around her throat, a cigar balanced between two fingers like she was channeling some forbidden old-Hollywood legend.

    * A goddamn fantasy. *

    Darcy gasped like she'd just caught a priest shoplifting lingerie.

    “Diva, are you insane? Did you even think before you double-tapped this?” Her grin stretched wide, shock shining in her eyes. “How many times did you look at this?” “Yes” Rio muttered, burying her face in her hands.

    Darcy lit up like a Christmas tree. “Holy shit” she whispered, delighted. “You totally DJed your bean over this masc version of our boss.”

    Rio groaned, tipping her head back in her chair like distance could somehow cancel out the humiliation crawling under her skin.

    “Can we not do this right now?”

    But her friend was unstoppable. One hand to her chest, the other clapped dramatically over her mouth, like Rio had just confessed to murder.

    “You did! You absolutely did!”

    She darted a glance around the room, scandalized, her voice pitching high. “I can’t even look at you right now. This is our boss, Rio. Our boss. You sit across from her in meetings, taking notes, nodding like a good little employee, and then you go home and defile her photos like some feral little goblin?”

    She whirled back with wicked glee.

    “You’re worse than a man.”

    And while ruffling Rio’s hair like she was patting a particularly filthy stray, she added “A disgusting little freak, that's what you are.”

    Rio shut her eyes. She drew a breath. Tried not to choke on the avalanche of mortification and jealousy clawing at her ribs. She was one hashtag away from losing her grip. Darcy didn’t mean to be cruel. That was the worst part.

    She was just… having fun. Babbling, teasing, oblivious.

    Peppering Rio with commentary about the one woman she still hadn’t managed to scrape off her skin.

    Her friend gasped again, clutching Rio’s arm like she’d struck gold a second time. “Oh my God, have you seen her replies? She flirts back.”

    * For God’s sake. This was hell. Had she died at her desk and gone straight to her custom- made damnation? *

    Darcy read silently for a beat, breathless.

    “Wow. Wow. Wow. That’s filthy.”

    Another beat.

    “Reaper’s got game, let me tell you.”

    Scroll, scroll.

    “Yep. She’s got it. No question.”

    As if she were judge and jury, stamping approval on Agatha’s smooth replies to strangers, and not-so-strangers.

    * Oh, Agatha had GAME. *

    Rio knew it better than anyone. She’d been on the receiving end. She knew the danger, the thrill. The way Agatha looked at you - not just saw you, but studied you. Pursued you. Haunted you.

    Without warning, Darcy’s tone softened.

    “Aww. Wait, who’s this little guy?”

    Rio’s head snapped up.

    Her friend wasn’t scrolling thirst anymore. She held the phone in both hands, brows lifted, gaze gone tender.

    On screen: a video. A bunny. Ears flopping over his ridiculous face, nose twitching, tiny paws fumbling for a treat.

    Rio’s throat locked.

    “She posted a video of Scratchy?” she whispered, before she could stop herself. Darcy blinked, surprised. “You know her rabbit’s name?”

    Rio looked away too fast. “She’s posted him before. A couple times.”

    A lie. Just another one in the long list of things she’d hidden about Agatha from her best friend.

    Because Agatha had never shared Scratchy on her public feed. Not once. Rio hadn’t seen Scratchy online.

    She’d met him.

    Held him.

    Fed him.

    Let him chew the frayed cuff of her hoodie while Agatha leaned against the doorway, watching with that rare, unguarded smile that made Rio feel wanted. Safe. And that memory cut deeper than all the thirst comments combined.

    “I didn’t peg her for a bunny girl” Darcy said lightly, still watching the video. “I can’t even picture her petting something.”

    Rio said nothing. Because what could she say?

    That she knew exactly how it felt to be petted by Agatha Harkness? That Agatha was the hottest, most devastating, most terrifying owner a pet could ever fall for? No. There was nothing to say. Not in front of Darcy. Not with her lungs filling with razors. Not when the bunny - of all things - was what finally broke her.

    Her breathing went shallow. Chest tight. Panic clawing at her throat. The last thing she needed was for her oblivious friend to notice.

    So she muttered, “Mind if we finish this at home? I need to wrap this scene before I leave.” Her voice sounded calm. Flat. But her pulse was slamming against her windpipe like her heart wanted out.

    Not the most graceful way to kick her best friend out of her office, but it would have to do. She couldn’t stop replaying it: the way Agatha, perched on her desk, had called her my love. This time intentional. Conscious. The desperate plea of go back to the kissing in the middle of an argument. And now? Now Agatha was what? Working her way through every flawless woman in sight? Like those words had meant nothing. Like Rio had imagined the whole damn thing.

    What a fucking liar.

    “Oh, sure, sure” Darcy scrambled up from the armchair, cheeks pink. “Sorry, dude. Didn’t mean to break the genius vibe. I’ll wait downstairs.”

    “No worries. You never interrupt” Rio forced a smile she didn’t feel. She needed space. Silence. Anything but witnesses. “But this is gonna take me a while. Just head home. I’ll meet you there.”

    “You sure?”

    “Totally. Don’t worry, I’ll Uber there ”

    Darcy grinned, gave a little wave. “Oh, right. Forgot we’re fancy now. Big-girl paychecks.” She tugged the door shut behind her.

    The office fell quiet.

    Rio didn’t even pretend to keep writing. The half-finished page sat abandoned as her head spun, orbit locked on one name: Agatha.

    Maybe it was recklessness. Maybe masochism. Either way, her hand moved on autopilot, pulling out her phone. Darcy had been right, notifications waited. Agatha had liked some of her posts.

    That did it.

    No scrolling this time.

    Straight to DMs.

    VidaldeRio: tf u doing liking my posts??

    Her thumb hit send before her brain caught up.

    Instant regret followed. Too late.

    The reply came almost immediately. Seconds. Like Agatha had been waiting. MotherHarkness: professional interest There it was. That voice Rio could hear even through text - dry, impossible, dipped in venom and amusement. A smirk in words.

    VidaldeRio: lame excuse MotherHarkness: ok, fine. Call it artistic analysis Mockery. Pure mockery. Rio should’ve known better. She always should’ve known better. But Agatha had a way of making her forget self-preservation entirely.

    VidaldeRio: cut the crap MotherHarkness: what was ur excuse scrolling back n liking all my old shit these past months? i might steal it * Shit. She knew. She’d noticed those likes. The ones from way before they ever touched. * Rio froze. No comeback, no clever save. Cornered, she defaulted to the classic wounded insult.

    VidaldeRio: ur such a pain in the ass MotherHarkness: harsh VidaldeRio: deserved u aren't supposed 2 act like this MotherHarkness: oh yeah? and how exactly am i supposed 2 act?

    go on. school me.

    * What the actual fuck? A command, dressed up as curiosity!? Told you. GAME * Both turned on and out of breath, Rio forced herself to answer with faux formality. VidaldeRio: idk. different. better MotherHarkness: different how?? better than who??

    sounds like the real me doesn’t line up w/ the fantasy u built in ur head. There it was again, psychological vivisection. But that’s what she’d signed up for: falling for a modern-day gangster hiding behind a producer’s mask.

    And in a way, Agatha wasn’t wrong. Rio had built illusions around her, illusions her lover never once pretended to maintain.

    VidaldeRio: know what? ur right.

    bc at this point… i honestly got no clue who u even are.

    MotherHarkness: easy fix. wanna know how?

    The question landed like a loaded gun.

    Her fingers tightened around the phone. She exhaled hard.

    VidaldeRio: whatever not in the mood 4 ur shameless flirting rn.

    That should’ve been the end. Slam the door. Leave her hanging.

    But Agatha didn’t take it that way.

    MotherHarkness: sooo what r u in the mood for?

    The words sat there. Invasive. Impossible to ignore.

    Rio stared until they blurred. She could block her. Close the app. Choose silence. She didn’t.

    VidaldeRio: nothing A long beat. Then, against her better judgment: VidaldeRio: It's been a long fuckin' day Agatha’s reply came quick.

    MotherHarkness: why? what happened?

    VidaldeRio: boring work shit. nothing worth talking about.

    MotherHarkness: tell me anyway i wanna hear Those last texts, all neatly contained in their text bubbles, shifted the vibe, steering the conversation somewhere unexpectedly intimate.
