    Chapter 22: I Exist in Two Places, Here and Where You Are or

    The One Where We Ponder 'If Villain Bad, Why Villain Hot?'

    Chapter Summary 1 (smug as hell) extreme overthinker + 1 Type-A hustler (violently impulsive) = ? Apply PEMDAS accordingly.

    Chapter Notes Here it is. Late, but written with the same love and feral energy as always. Thank you for your patience.

    See the end of the chapter for more notes Lately, what Rio felt, what she said, and what she did, especially where love and relationships were concerned, rarely aligned.

    Over the past few months, she learned to live inside that fracture with unnerving ease: self- improving and self-destructive at once. Disciplined and reckless in the same breath. She couldn’t have explained how it worked. It simply did.

    But the contradictions were no longer content to remain theoretical.

    They were growing louder.

    Harder to justify.

    Harder to keep neatly contained.

    They demanded space. Noise. Consequence.

    Right now, the last contradiction surfaced in a room that wasn’t hers while the headboard laid siege to the wall in a merciless rhythm. Each impact was a blunt reminder that the control she believed she had over her own life had never been real. Only borrowed. Drywall shuddered.

    The bed answered back.

    Again and again.

    Soon came a sound that cut through everything else. Ragged, stripped of pretense. Desperate. Unguarded.

    “Oh my... I'm...I’m gonna...RIO!”

    May’s breath faltered. Her fingers clenched the sheets, knuckles whitening as the miracle in her bed drove her efficently through the final, brutal crest of release. The mattress sighed beneath them when Rio finally collapsed at the cougar's side, muscles slack, pulse still racing. Sweat glinting faintly at her temple.

    And then… silence.

    Brittle.

    Almost artificial.

    The air between them lingered heavy and unsettled, the only evidence anything had happened at all. The encounter had ended too quickly, too neatly, like a scene staged for efficiency rather than desire. An imitation of passion that skimmed the surface and never once reached the bone.

    “Wow” May murmured at last, breaking it. “That was intense.”

    Her breath was still uneven, a tentative smile tugging at her mouth as she reached for the sheets and drew them up over their bodies.

    A small, unnecessary gesture of tenderness. Warmth offered out of habit, not intimacy. Something misplaced. Something that didn’t belong here, and certainly not something Rio had ever imagined sharing with her.

    They’d only done this a handful of times. Each time had been fine. Good, even. But never anything that asked to be remembered.

    Her body had answered, yes. But Rio’s heart, her mind, her soul, had never even been in the room.

    May was a patch.

    A stopgap.

    A blurry, insufficient placeholder.

    For her.

    For the exquisite, hell-born disruption that refused to loosen its grip. That walking desecration of grace. A catastrophe shaped like a woman.

    The only one.

    Over the last few days, Rio had been forced to admit what she had spent months denying: she had never truly escaped that force of nature. And some dark, masochistic part of her had never wanted to.

    Because what she and that demon had shared hadn’t been sex alone. It had been magick. Alchemy. Passion transmuted into something incandescent.

    Dangerous. Unstable. Impossible to contain.

    Their nights together were reactions under pressure: heat, force, bodies driven past endurance until the impact forged something irreversible. Sex that burned and saved at once. Apocalyptic not because it erased them, but because it left them altered beyond repair. When that blasphemy-made-flesh touched her, Rio - and the world - didn’t bend. They detonated.

    Bedsheets, headboards, the illusion of restraint, everything collapsed the moment that beautiful liar’s body met hers.

    Because nothing about Agatha was ever tentative.

    She claimed.

    Devoured.

    Unmade.

    Furniture didn’t splinter. It yielded.

    Blankets didn’t slide to the floor. They fled, ripped violently out of the equation. And the bed was never a setting; it was collateral damage in a war waged with teeth and want. A cathedral collapsing under the weight of the purest temptation Rio had ever known. Nothing between them had ever been containable.

    It was ruin masquerading as intimacy.

    Violence disguised as worship.

    A holy, hedonistic devastation built for two.

    Nothing measured.

    Nothing safe.

    And certainly nothing that could be folded away and hidden sweetly beneath cotton sheets patterned with harmless little shapes like these.

    So this quiet, this soft landing...felt wrong.

    Foreign.

    Tame It lingered like a misprint. An accidental stillness where there should have been heat. Rupture. Some heavy aftershock to mark the moment.

    Instead, the room felt scrubbed clean of chaos and replaced with something palatable. Inoffensive.

    Something that didn’t fit Rio at all, nor what she needed.

    But maybe this was exactly what she’d bargained for: A warm body to ferry her through the dead space between Friday nights and Monday mornings. A serviceable stand-in for the woman her mind refused to stop conjuring. Something to occupy her hands, her hours, her thoughts.

    Someone who wasn’t Agatha.

    May - the imitation, the temporary solution - knew fragments of the truth. She knew Rio was tangled in a complicated situationship she refused to elaborate on.

    So far, that had been enough for her.

    Right now, as her breathing evened out, she looked not just content, but unmistakably satisfied.

    Her smile was open. Uncalculated.

    For all her steel at the office, for all that Agatha-ish confidence she wore so convincingly, she looked almost too sweet now.

    “Thank you. I needed that” she whispered, pressing a soft kiss to Rio’s mouth. With the unhurried trust of someone who believed tenderness was renewable, something you could offer freely without consequence, she shifted closer and rested her head against her new lover's chest, as if the space had always belonged to her.

    Caught off guard by the sudden, uninvited closeness, Rio lifted an arm and covered her eyes, exhaling slowly into the darkness behind her lids as May settled there. The bed was warm.

    The lights were low.

    Dawn hovered just beyond the wall-to-wall window, not quite ready to claim the room. The quiet ran deep enough to pass for peace.

    All of it should have felt comforting.

    Safe, even, if hollow.

    Instead, the moment clung to her like borrowed clothing: the wrong cut, the wrong weight, the persistent itch of something tailored for someone else.

    Fishing for a compliment, May leaned in close, her breath warming Rio’s neck as she murmured half teasing, half sincere “You’re probably thinking I’m too old for you.” A joke.

    An offering.

    A tentative reach beyond uncomplicated sex, toward something perilously close to connection.

    A door Rio could not, and would not, walk through.

    A faint, involuntary smirk touched that walking red flag's mouth before she could stop it. No.

    She wasn’t thinking about May at all.

    If she’d been worrying about age gaps or power dynamics or expiration dates, at least she would have been present with the woman resting on her chest.

    But she wasn’t.

    Her thoughts - treacherous, stubborn, wholly uninvited - kept circling back to the one force she had never managed to outrun. The comparison rose whether she wanted it or not. Because if Agatha had been in this bed, in this neatly arranged post-sex quiet, stillness would never have survived for long.

    Oh, no.

    That wicked, magnetic, ungovernable woman would have already rolled on top of her, all confidence and inevitability, making surrender feel less like a choice and more like a law of nature. As if Rio’s yielding had never been a matter of will at all, only physics. Something written into her body long before Agatha ever touched her. Something that responded to that woman as if it had been built for no one else.

    Even now, months later, all Rio had to do was close her eyes and the best view of her entire damn life rebuilt itself in the dark without effort.

    Because nothing, absolutely nothing, eclipsed the sight of that gorgeous problem above her. The memory was flawless. Unmatched.

    It surfaced with humiliating ease, polished by repetition, revisited far more often than she ever allowed herself to admit: That relentless, godless disaster of a lover leaning in close enough for her breath to ghost down her neck, murmuring my turn - low, unhurried, pitched with precision to make her shiver.

    Mischief and hunger braided together in that feral, delighted grin.

    The quick flash of her tongue between her teeth like a private joke meant only for the woman beneath her. A prelude. A warning of exactly how thoroughly she intended to undo her. Always accompanied by that glint of lethal delight in her eyes, as if daring the universe to try and stop her from fucking Rio senseless in payment for every touch already given. And that hair, always the hair, tossed back with infuriatingly unhurried grace, allowed to fall over one shoulder in a theatrical cascade, like a curtain lifting just before the real show began.

    Because desire, in Agatha’s hands, had never been accidental. It was engineered. Assembled with care. A slow, deliberate ignition she stepped into willingly, and then released, feeding on her lover with an ease that felt almost elemental.

    She didn’t simply feel passion; she shaped it. Directed it. Claimed it. And only then did she allow herself, and Rio, to sink into the fire she had so meticulously summoned. It should have felt artificial. A spectacle. Too staged to be real.

    Instead, it made everything between them unbearable in its truth. As if the performance were merely a necessary, inevitable threshold into something too vast, too intimate to face without ritual. Without disguise.

    If what Rio felt for that living requiem had been only attraction, life might have been kinder. She might have outgrown it.

    Sweated it out.

    Buried it under May’s warm, uncomplicated wanting.

    Her new lover should have helped.

    She was supposed to reset the equation.

    A clean variable.

    Instead, Rio had been using her as a temporary bandage, stretched thin over a wound she refused to admit was still bleeding.

    And the longer she leaned on her coworker as a solution, the clearer the truth became: There was no remedy for what she felt for Agatha.

    Because this wasn’t infatuation. Not limerence. Not one of those embarrassing romantic fixations.

    This was absence.

    And Agatha’s absence wasn’t shaped like another woman. It wasn’t even shaped like pain. It was something far more unmanageable - a vast, warped gravity well, swallowing every tentative feeling Rio tried to grow in its vicinity before it had the chance to take hold. Expecting May to fill that kind of void hadn’t just been naive. It had been cruel, from the very beginning.

    That didn’t mean Rio failed to see her clearly, or to recognize what she brought to the table. She was impressive in all the ways that were supposed to matter.

    In the way she moved through the world with unshakeable confidence, as if she’d always been told she was enough. Grounded. Self-assured. Occasionally dark, but only in that well- adjusted, therapist-approved way of people who had done the work and come out intact on the other side.

    And yes, she was beautiful. Flawless skin. A great face. An easy smile. A killer body, spectacular tits included.

    And still...

    She was only a palate cleanser. And a thin one at that.

    Like rinsing your mouth with water after whiskey.

    The burn lingered.

    The aftertaste stayed.

    And the craving for something stronger - someone darker, more dangerous - never truly left. Months of self-preserving denial had failed to dull the central fact of Rio’s existence: she carried an almost humiliating need for Agatha, and for Agatha’s approval. For her to think she was exceptional. Brilliant. Devastatingly funny. Impossible to ignore. She needed to be seen by her. Chosen by her. Taken seriously by her. And she needed it with a hunger that ignored dignity, dismissed logic, and never slept.

    But that need didn’t erase memory.

    It didn’t soften the damage.

    She remembered, vividly, the casual cruelty. The exquisite carelessness with which that modern, breathtaking Judas had hurt her, had cracked her open like a lock forced too quickly, spilling every foolish, romantic instinct she’d worked so hard to keep contained. Rio knew exactly who she was obsessed with.

    A perfect con artist.

    A woman capable of offering the illusion of devotion with one hand while quietly pocketing Rio’s needs with the other.

    No one who genuinely cared about Rio would ever have called Agatha Harkness a suitable partner.

    They would have been right. Entirely.

    And still, during that brief, incendiary stretch of time they had shared, Agatha had given her something no one else ever had.

    Something worth kneeling for. Worth aching for. Worth undoing herself over. That was the problem.

    That had always been the problem.

    Agatha was far from perfect.

    And what they’d had was neither safe nor healthy. Rio understood that better than anyone alive.

    And yet the truth that had lodged itself in her bones the instant their eyes collided in that stupid, mirrored elevator remained immovable: Agatha was perfect for her.

    Nearly a full minute passed with Rio stranded in her own thoughts, May’s self-deprecating comment hanging unanswered between them.

    She didn’t reply.

    Not because she was distracted or drifting, but because she’d gone still in a very specific way. Guarded. Defensive. A practiced silence designed to protect what she wasn’t willing to give. The PG-13 version of Agatha sensed it immediately and let the moment go. She didn’t push. Didn’t ask again. Only offered a small, polite smile before reaching for her phone on the nightstand, her thumb already scrolling before her head had fully settled back against the pillow.

    Within seconds, the consultant-showrunner was discussing budget strategies for the Lady Death finale. Voice calm, precise, professional. As if the bed beneath them hadn’t been rattling against the wall moments earlier. As if she hadn’t just admitted, plainly, without accusation, that Rio’s energy overwhelmed her.

    While she disappeared into numbers and contingencies, Rio stayed flat on her back, staring at the ceiling. Her chest was still rising too quickly for how quiet the room had become and her muscles still humming from the workout of topping May.

    Her gaze snagged on the hanging lamp overhead. Awoven rattan piece, faintly bohemian, utterly out of place in a Malibu house. She wondered if May had brought it from New York, or bought it here in an attempt to look less like the typical Hollywood soulless prick. Darcy would love it. Her birthday was coming up.

    She filed the thought away, making a mental note to take a picture later. The chime of a text sliced clean through her reverie.

    Adrenaline flared bright and immediate.

    Rio sat up too fast, swung her legs over the edge of the bed. Her bare feet met the cool, polished wood.

    She stood even faster, hissing under her breath when her hurried first step sent her pinky toe clipping the bedframe.

    The oversized T-shirt still clung to her. The one May had tried to tug over her head earlier, before Rio, unwilling to meet her eyes, had flipped her onto the mattress and taken her from behind. Now it lay damp against her spine, sweat pressing the fabric into her ribs. She tugged it down just enough to cover herself.

    Reflex. Not modesty.

    With the right people, Rio was uninhibited, almost feral. She moved through the world with instinctive confidence, inhabiting her body without apology, trusting it to know where it belonged and how much space it was allowed to take.

    But she was also deeply sensitive.

    A seemingly contradictory combination - one that should have been counterproductive - but she’d learned, through hard practice, how to make it work.

    With the wrong people, she went quiet.

    Not timid. Not uncertain. Just unreachable.

    She didn’t disappear, not exactly. She still occupied the room, still moved with the same unstudied confidence. But she spoke less. Her voice flattened. Her body closed ranks. Something essential withdrew behind her eyes, leaving behind a version of herself that was polite, agreeable, faintly distant.

    A decoy.

    Most people never noticed the difference. They mistook ease for openness, humor for intimacy. They saw the grin, the irreverence, the way she filled space when she chose to, and assumed they’d been invited in.

    They hadn’t.

    If her intuition marked you as unworthy of that access, she stayed on the surface. Pleasant. Entertaining. Untouched. And no amount of proximity would change that. Because Rio didn’t reveal herself by degrees. She didn’t offer fragments or negotiate closeness in installments. The decision was immediate and instinctive, a quiet internal verdict rendered on first contact. Either you were allowed to see her.

    Or you weren’t.

    That was why she kept her tattoos covered.

    Each one traced a fault line, moments that had split her open and rearranged her from the inside out. Pain translated into image. Joy sharpened into permanence. They weren’t decoration. They weren’t part of the charismatic armor she’d built to survive a life that had rarely been gentle with her.

    They were proof.

    History written directly onto her skin.

    May, like most people, hadn’t earned those stories. So the mask stayed on, in the form of a T- shirt.

    With the hem adjusted, stretched to fall just below the curve of her ass, Rio crossed the vast bedroom and retrieved her jeans from where they’d been abandoned near the window. She slid them on and fished her phone from the back pocket.

    Only then did she pause and glanced out through the wall-to-wall glass. A beutiful beach stretched beyond it, unreal, like a billionaire’s screensaver. The ocean lay dark and polished, catching the first thin threads of morning light. The house itself was a study in coastal minimalism and relaxed luxury.

    Rio took it in with mild, detached curiosity.

    It was the first time she’d spent the night here.

    Usually, she fucked May at the office. Or took her back to her own place. Familiar ground. Controlled variables.

    Agatha’s friend had taste, she’d give her that.

    Or an excellent designer.

    Same difference.

    Her thumb brushed the screen awake.

    Notifications bloomed: emails, spam.

    And, inevitably, her best friend’s latest masterpiece: a frantic message from the night before, begging her not to come home because she had a guy over and was planning a full tantric experience, apparently timed to climax at tonight’s premiere.

    The message was saturated with explicit emojis, enough to make Rio consider outlawing the peach forever and rinsing her retinas with bleach.

    She ignored all of it and opened the only message that mattered.

    The one that had just arrived, searing in its simplicity.

    She told herself, as she always did when that familiar, fatal indulgence reached back for her, that it meant nothing. That it was just Agatha maintaining control. Keeping her within reach. Leaving the door ajar in case she ever decided to pull her back into her bed. That she texted because she was bored. Or lonely. Or because powerful women, when left unattended, inevitably went looking for a distraction - something warm and responsive to pass the time.

    Agatha crouched beside the corpse. Even at such close range, she felt no revulsion, only the familiar irritation she reserved for things that wasted her time.

    “What a spectacular pain in my ass you turned out to be” she said conversationally, as if addressing a malfunctioning appliance rather than a dead woman.

    “You made such a mess. Months of games. Months of agitation. All that… just to rot in a ditch like spoiled produce.”

    The body offered no rebuttal. This wasn’t Dottie anymore. Not even the echo of the role she’d tried so hard to inhabit. Just meat that had once talked too much. Agatha let the silence stretch, then added, almost thoughtfully, “Well. One less sanctimonious parasite in the world.”

    The words carried no heat. No triumph. Just tidy accounting.

    Behind her, her benefactor released a quiet, incredulous laugh.

    “I’ve always admired your staggering callousness, Agatha.”

    Even with death cooling at her feet, Agatha Harkness pulled focus. Irreverent, unrepentant, magnetic as ever.

    The woman didn’t look up. Just let a thin smile curve her mouth and accepted the backhanded compliment with the same courtesy one reserves for an overdue bill. Polite, impersonal, faintly annoyed.

    Admiration, after all, was just another form of misunderstanding.

    The smile lingered. Familiar. Dangerous.

    “Honestly, it was only a matter of time” she said, rising to her feet and brushing mud from her coat as if the universe had just resolved a minor administrative inconvenience on her behalf.

    The words dropped between them like stones. Heavy, inelegant.

    Her expression didn’t soften. If anything, it sharpened.

    Making no effort to hide the quiet satisfaction Dottie’s death brought her. Agatha had despised her long before that harpy ever declared open war.

    She recognized the cruelty in that satisfaction. But cruelty was a tool. And she had always known how to use her tools well.

    If Elektra’s people handled the cleanup properly, there might still be something salvageable here. Information. Leverage. Loose threads worth tugging.

    Her shadow investor studied her now with narrowed eyes, suspicion tightening her features, something hovering between disbelief and accusation.

    “Yeah, she might as well have painted a target on her forehead”

    From her tone, and the slow way her gaze tracked her, it was painfully clear Elektra wasn’t talking about fate.

    She meant Agatha.

    And it wasn’t an unreasonable conclusion.

    After all, there in the mud lay Agatha’s most recent nemesis: Dottie Jones. Or, according to the suspiciously pristine driver’s license pulled from her pocket, Sarah Proctor.

    The name didn’t matter. The woman barely did. What lingered was the damage she’d left behind. Corrosive, petty, and self-righteous. Dottie had been the sort of hypocrite who preached about clean work environments while wading through the same filth as everyone else, never with more finess, just louder condemnation and a pastel sweater thrown over the rot. A contagion wrapped in condescending smiles, the sort who thought morality could be cataloged, color-coded, and weaponized.

    She called her accusations Evidence of malpractice and corruption.

    Agatha called them Witch hunts.

    She could still picture her perfectly: self-satisfied to the point of parody, preening in her so- called decency, clipped, like she’d stepped straight out of a lifestyle catalog. Brittle in that upper-middle-class way. Lacquered. Hollow. Polishing her moral superiority like a medal she’d never earned.

    Still a rat, though.

    Just a slippery one.

    A rat who thought she could vanish into a non-coastal California town and cosplay domestic virtue - gingham curtains, soft-focus makeup, calling herself a trad wife - while quietly hoarding and selling Westview Productions’ most sensitive files to the highest bidder, convinced she was some kind of crusader.

    But Agatha was exceptionally good at finding lost things.

    Once she located the nest, the demolition became both art and discipline. Months of pressure applied with icy precision. Every move calibrated to rupture Dottie’s carefully curated new life without ever laying a finger on her. Every consequence orchestrated without slipping outside the law.

    Eviction notices blooming like poisonous flowers.

    Bank accounts sealed shut. Frozen.

    Credit fossilized.

    A husband terminated on cue, dismissed as effortlessly as flicking ash from a cigarette. Agatha unspooled Dottie’s life thread by thread until there was nothing left to cling to. That snake’s little rebellion against the L.A. status quo had been her fatal mistake. She’d picked the wrong rich bitch to piss off.

    She hadn’t just stolen Westview Productions files.

    She’d been the reason Agatha lost her most precious pet.

    And worse, she’d dragged Nicky into Hollywood’s petty power games, believing – astonishingly - that she could get away with it.

    Agatha’s retaliation had unfolded beautifully. Clean. Measured. Inevitable. Seemingly untraceable.

    Until last Thursday.

    That was when Dottie came undone in the Westview lobby. Desperate, shrill. Screaming that the Head Producer was a fraud. A pest. That she was ruining her life. As though what was happening wasn’t simply the logical conclusion of her own choices. She begged.

    She invoked the existence of a daughter.

    She dropped to her knees when security arrived, clinging to the delusion that humiliation could purchase mercy.

    As if that could change anything.

    As if Agatha weren’t merely responding with the ferocity of any mother protecting her own. Maybe snapping publicly at the woman’s mere presence on her territory, and loudly threatening to bury her so deep the worms would need a map, hadn’t been Agatha’s most diplomatic moment.

    She knew that.

    Then again, Dottie should have known better than to parade herself as a wounded saint in front of someone who didn’t believe in redemption. Someone who, once set in motion, finished exactly what she started.

    While the operatives lifted the body onto a gurney, Agatha began to circle the clearing. She traced the perimeter with slow steps, cataloguing angles, distances, blind spots. Her mind moved faster than her body, collapsing old strategies and erecting new ones with the cold efficiency of habit.

    This was a complication. Not a catastrophe.

    Yet.

    She was already halfway through drafting an internal protocol she hoped she wouldn’t need when something caught her eye.

    A flicker of reflected light.

    Small. Metallic.

    Half-submerged in a shallow pool of mud near the corpse.

    Her stride faltered.

    Her breath stalled. Not dramatically, but completely, as if her body had simply forgotten what came next.

    * No. No. Absolutely not. *

    It was impossible.

    Her cameo.

    Her family heirloom.

    Just lying there.

    Agatha crouched slowly, as if the ground itself might recoil if she moved too fast. Her gloved fingers trembled despite her discipline, despite years of training herself out of visible reactions. The oval shape was unmistakable even before she touched it. The chain had snapped clean through.

    Mud clung to the enamel in thick, obscuring streaks. She wiped it against her jeans, once, twice, until a muted cobalt sheen emerged beneath the filth. Three pale figures revealed themselves in a familiar configuration: Maiden. Mother. Crone.

    Recognition locked something cold and immovable in her chest.

    Exposure.

    Again.

    This was proof the murder hadn’t been random.

    This wasn’t sloppy.

    It was personal.

    A message delivered intentionally. A taunt calibrated specifically for her. A threat delivered with craft.

    Whoever had done this hadn’t merely killed Dottie Jones and walked away. They had staged the aftermath with care.

    They didn’t just want a body found.

    They wanted the Reaper framed for it.

    Frankly, it was impressive. Elegant. Theatrical.

    A solid ten out of ten on the intimidation scale. Light-years beyond the tired vulgarity of a horse’s head in a bed.

    Her thoughts fractured, racing.

    * When had she last worn the cameo? *

    The question lodged in her like a thorn. And memory, cruel and obedient, rose to meet it. First came the afterimage of a meeting that had demanded more restraint than it deserved. May had just left, her heels cracking down the corridor, still yapping about something Agatha had already dismissed as irrelevant.

    She standing in the doorway of her office, one hand resting on the handle. Her posture was immaculate.

    Her pulse was anything but.

    Because Rio - leather pants, lilac sleeveless tank top, no bra Rio - hadn’t left yet. Agatha had perfected professionalism in her presence. Months of composure. Civility carefully rehearsed and precisely deployed.

    Most days, it held.

    But that day, it took everything she had not to close the distance when Rio approached with that infuriatingly soft, almost sheepish smile, as if genuinely surprised by the effect she had simply by existing in her office dressed like that. As if she hadn’t spent the entire meeting watching Agatha’s mouth, her throat, her hands. Eyes lingering a beat too long each time, dark and glossy with intent.

    Agatha had imagined contact. Wanted it.

    She hadn’t expected it.

    But as that tour de force of a human being stepped past her, her fingers brushed her neck. Her collarbone. Barely there. A touch so light it should have meant nothing, and somehow said everything.

    It wasn’t accidental.

    And it wasn’t innocent.

    The faint hitch in Rio’s breath, the familiar nervous stutter that surfaced only when she was close to losing control, told her exactly what it meant. Months of careful waiting had reached their limit.

    The waiting was over.

    Her pet was past denial now. She wanted her back.

    Wanted the leash again.

    Wanted to feel it tighten.

    Agatha stood frozen there long after that beautiful problem had gone, the door still open. Her eyes closed. Her fingers rising instinctively to her collarbone, to the cameo resting there, where Rio had nudged it back into place with infuriating gentleness, as if sensation could echo, as if touch might linger by sheer force of will.

    But no.

    That hadn’t been the last time she wore the necklace.

    It had been Sunday.

    The beach.

    A pale winter sun warming her son’s face. Salt in the air. The tide pulling gently, insistently, as if it had all the time in the world. A rare, fragile pocket of peace in a life that rarely allowed such luxuries.

    They had been lying on a towel, talking about nothing in particular. Nicky’s fingers had found the pendant absently, affectionately, tugging at it as he laughed. Agatha had reached over to fix his ponytail, smoothing a few escaped strands, smiling at something he said, some small joke, some harmless tease.

    And now...

    Here it was.

    In the mud.

    Beside a corpse.

    * Had she lost it? Or had someone taken it? *

    Her pulse quickened.

    She closed her fist around the pendant, rose smoothly to her feet, and slipped it into her pocket.

    The game had just escalated.

    This was another secret to bury. Another lie to construct. Another truth Elektra could never be allowed to glimpse.

    A crow cawed from a nearby branch.

    The sound was ugly. Harsh. Insistent.

    Agatha looked up in time to see it watching her, head cocked, black eyes unblinking. A chill traced her spine. Not fear. Not superstition.

    Recognition.

    A bad omen.

    The fine hairs at the nape of her neck rose.

    For a second, the forest seemed to hold its breath.

    And clarity struck. Sudden, precise.

    Oh, now she knew exactly who had killed this...Sarah Something.

    Or, at the very least, who had ordered it.

    Agatha stripped off her gloves, clapped her hands once as if dispersing whatever residue still clung to her skin, and walked toward the silent backer of this whole operation, who stood several paces away, absorbed in a low-voiced briefing with her operatives. They met halfway.

    “We can’t make her disappear, and we can’t pass her off as a Jane Doe. We move the body. Nothing more” Elektra stated evenly, without preamble.

    “When someone finally recognizes her, they’ll put a name to that face” she continued. “And when they do...”

    She let the words settle, gave them just enough space to bloom into consequence. Agatha finished the sentence for her, tone calm, almost indulgent. “...they’ll come for me.” Her mouth curved, not quite into a smile. It was the expression of someone already accounting for the fallout, and finding it tolerable. The look of a woman three steps ahead, surveying the damage with professional interest.

    “But we can control when she resurfaces, can’t we?” Agatha went on, conversational, as if this were a matter of optics rather than a body waiting to be found.

    Their eyes locked.

    No theatrics. No posturing. Just the quiet, efficient understanding of women who had cleaned blood from their hands often enough to know how long stains really took to set. “A little” Elektra conceded, tapping her phone with a gloved finger. “Given her condition, the margin’s thin.”

    “How thin?”

    “You fly tomorrow morning. Be there on time.”

    A chime cut cleanly through the clearing. Agatha’s phone, the one reserved for uglier business, lit up. A location dropped into her inbox.

    She exhaled a soft, displeased scoff.

    As a businesswoman, she despised setbacks, particularly when the finish line was already smoldering within reach.

    Tomorrow was too soon. She’d expected at least the usual forty-eight hours. She loathed rushed cover-ups. They always failed the same way: sloppily, loudly. Art required time. Precision. The patience to hunt down every loose thread before it could unravel the entire design.

    And above all, she hated being ordered.

    “Five a.m. Not a second later, Harkness” Elektra pressed, as if she could read the defiance behind Agatha’s eyes. “The day after tomorrow is going to be a shitshow.” In this arrangement, she was the capital. And capital, as they both understood, functioned like muscle.

    So Agatha said nothing. Silence, she had learned, could pass for acquiescence when deployed correctly. She lifted her chin instead, irritation tightening her jaw. “Use these hours wisely” her accomplice continued. “Remember, no loose ends.” “The best way to ensure that is to let me get back to work”

    She was done with this place. The mud. The body. The interruption masquerading as fate. She needed distance. Space. Time to recalibrate and prepare for what was already in motion. Elektra shifted her stance, angling her body so the operatives lingering among the trees couldn’t read her lips.

    “Tame the Witch, please” she said quietly, tilting her phone just enough for Agatha to see. “It would be… inconvenient if she decided to cooperate with S.H.I.E.L.D.” Her thumb moved.

    The first images were a few months old.

    Wanda Maximoff at the cemetery, black coat still stiff with newness, grief raw and unprocessed. Agent Johnson standing a little too close. Agent May a step behind, notebook already open. Wanda’s face caught mid-blink. Disoriented. Hollow. Nowhere near ready for questions.

    Then the timeline advanced.

    Different days. Different locations.

    Wanda intercepted on a sunlit sidewalk, confusion lagging just enough for Agent May to gain the upper hand.

    Another shot: Wanda frozen in her new apartment doorway, keys dangling uselessly as Agent Johnson’s badge caught the light.

    A café.

    A grocery store.

    Everyday errands, derailed with methodical consistency by the same two determined agents. The images kept coming.

    Wanda leaving Westview’s headquarters after yet another futile attempt to reconnect with Agatha. Shoulders tight, expression brittle, exhaustion etched deep. The same agents again. Patient. Persistent. Circling.

    A pattern.

    Elektra didn’t need to spell it out.

    Agatha didn’t blink.

    “She won’t” she stated coolly, cutting Elektra a warning glance.

    Her illegal partner waited a beat too long before adding, almost gently “And then there’s the other issue.”

    She didn’t say the name.

    She didn’t have to.

    In this line of work, secrets didn’t stay buried, they were merely redistributed. Especially among criminals.

    “What about her?”

    The uncomfortable truth was that Elektra believed desire had compromised Agatha’s judgment. She couldn’t fathom why a woman this ruthless, this methodical, was so intent on keeping a fragile-looking young writer safely outside the blast radius. Nor did she understand what still bound Agatha to a woman she was no longer sleeping with. The gravity of it. The devotion. The quiet, disciplined violence humming just beneath the surface.

    Most critically, she failed to grasp that Agatha Harkness’s latest indulgence was as dangerous as the Reaper herself.

    Like everyone else, Elektra had been taken in by Rio’s easy warmth. Mistook charm for harmlessness. Read sweetness where there was, in fact, something exquisitely lethal. But she understood enough not to threaten her.

    That would be a fatal miscalculation.

    She knew instinctively that if she, or anyone under her command, came too close to that girl, Agatha would respond by tearing the world apart. She would reduce them to something small and unrecognizable, hide the remains somewhere the world had learned not to look, and make it all appear accidental.

    Rio Vidal was a boundary you did not cross if you valued your life.

    So she chose restraint.

    “You might consider warning her” she said carefully. “They’ll try to reach her too.” Agatha’s voice didn’t rise.

    It dropped.

    Civility intact, but threaded now with something cold. Something faintly inhuman. “Dating advice? “From you?”

    That was the line.

    No escalation. No spectacle. Just a subtle recalibration of power.

    The threat had been acknowledged.

    And cleanly surpassed.

    Fear slid beneath Elektra’s skin like cold steel, a shiver she couldn’t quite suppress. She had no desire to provoke retaliation. No interest in watching this mean bitch dismantle her own vulnerabilities in response, likely beginning with pointed observations about Elektra’s favorite pro bono New York attorney.

    Exasperated, the diplomat’s daughter turned criminal pinched the bridge of her nose, a rare fissure in her otherwise immaculate composure.

    “One last thing” her voice cut cleanly through the trees just as Agatha reached her car. “Where were you last night?”

    A direct question. Stripped of diplomacy. Designed to determine whether Agatha had played any role at all in the murder cooling behind them.

    The Reaper paused, one hand already wrapped around the driver’s-side handle. She smiled, thin, precise, and did not turn around.

    “Busy.”

    That was all.

    No elaboration. No defensiveness.

    Elektra took a step closer, boots sinking slightly into the damp earth, and lowered her voice. The volume reserved for conversations meant never to echo.

    “If we determine this was personal and you failed to disclose it...”” she said carefully, each word placed like a chess piece.

    They both knew who we meant.

    The Five Fingers. The silent consortium that owned corporations, governments, supply chains, and entire economies, without ever standing for election or answering questions. People who did not tolerate surprises.

    Agatha turned then. Slowly. And met that necessary evil’s gaze without haste and asked, in a mild, almost curious tone, “Then what?”

    A beat.

    “What would you do?”

    It wasn’t bravado.

    It was a warning.

    Elektra had the resources. The infrastructure. The reach.

    But Agatha Harkness, architect of too many dowfalls to count, the unseen hand behind reputations ruined and empires quietly redirected, had something far more dangerous. She had the will.

    And the skill to use it without hesitation.

    For a long moment, no one moved, not the operatives positioned along the perimeter, not even the wind threading through the branches.

    Elektra’s gloved fingers twitched once around her phone.

    Her face remained composed but the faint, involuntary taps of her fingers against the casing betrayed her. A tell so small most people would miss it.

    She was performing calm. She always did with Agatha. It was the only strategy that had ever worked.

    Because the woman standing in front of her was not a colleague. Not an ally. Not even an asset in any meaningful sense of the word.

    She was a loaded weapon that occasionally chose to resemble a person. Agatha Harkness had been shaped by instinct and ambition, sharpened by a talent for persuasion that redirected lives and careers without ever making headlines. She did not conquer by force. She eroded. She rewrote incentives until people believed they had chosen their own ruin.

    And she would burn everything around her before bowing to anyone.

    Hollywood’s shadows belonged to her by right of conquest. She moved through them like breath through lungs: unseen, necessary, impossible to stop.

    Survival. Control. Manipulation.

    Those weren’t tactics she employed.

    They were what she was.

    And yet Agatha was a virtuoso at operating just beneath the threshold of notice. Her real power wasn't spectacle.

    It wasn't intimidation.

    It was invisibility.

    Influence exercised so cleanly it went unrecognized until the consequences were already irreversible.

    Elektra knew the woman standing there now in a bargain-bin plaid shirt, posture relaxed, expression almost indulgent, would never allow her sovereignty in Hollywood’s underbelly to be challenged. Not by money. Not by committees. Not by gods.

    She was a monster playing god inside a multibillion-dollar entertainment industry, doing it all with impeccable taste.

    Her backer could only hope that even nightmares still observed certain protocols. The silence thickened, alert and heavy, as though the clearing itself were waiting for permission to breathe.

    Agatha was the one who released it.

    She opened the car door, paused just long enough to glance back, and added. Almost as an afterthought, almost kind: “Well. I’ll leave you and your chumps to clean up this spectacular waste of my time.”

    The hem of her coat flared behind her as she slid into the driver’s seat. A dramatic flick of fabric that felt entirely intentional despite its casual timing. The door shut with a muted thud. The engine purred to life.

    And she drove away, leaving the clearing, the corpse, and every unspoken consequence behind her.

    By the time she reached the main road, one elbow resting against the open window, her temple pressed lightly to her knuckles, she caught herself humming another small, tuneless new melody Nicky had invented one day for no reason other than to make her smile. She’d noticed it had become a habit lately, something that surfaced whenever her thoughts began to outrun her control.

    She had taken precautions long before that opportunist had ended up face-down in the mud. Her son was protected as thoroughly as anyone could be in a world built on leverage, silence, and quiet violence. That part did not trouble her.

    So the humming steadied her.

    The headlights carved a pale tunnel through the fog, and with it, the calculations resumed. There was no ambiguity about what came next.

    The police would come for her.

    They would accuse her of killing that traitor.

    The sequence was predictable, almost dull. A choreography she had seen often enough to anticipate every step before it landed.

    Today would be nothing but damage control.

    She had calls to make. Angles to block. Alibis to stitch together. Bad choices to choose between, knowing full well that none of them would be clean. Because this time, time itself pressed against her throat.

    Less than twenty-four hours to pull everything tight and wrap it in something that passed for order.

    She organized her priorities the way she always did: cleanly, without sentiment. First: retrieve whatever Jones had hidden in the LTO vault. The room was enormous, a bureaucratic labyrinth of forgotten archives. And vanilla-scented, painfully average Dottie was clever enough to make sure the data wouldn’t give itself up easily. Second: deal with the redheaded complication once and for all. Wanda had been circling ever since the incident, no longer subtle, no longer patient. Intrusive. Nosy. Loudly convinced of her own relevance. The kind of problem that metastasized if left untreated. Third, and this one required finesse, warn Rio.

    Strangely enough, that was the most volatile variable of all.

    It was true that Rio had been… receptive lately. Softer than she used to be. Less cactus, more open bloom. But that didn’t mean Agatha wouldn’t get pricked when she finally explained the mess unfolding around them to a woman who had once accused her – accurately - of playing god with other people’s lives.

    The approach mattered. Timing mattered. Presentation mattered.

    Fortunately, she already had an outfit in mind. One that would command Rio’s full attention the moment they shared a room. She would also need to take a certain photo before leaving the house. Insurance, a visual anchor, in case Rio decided to be particularly stubborn. It wasn’t until she was home - Agnes’s ugly coat discarded over the back of a chair, her equally ugly shoes kicked off without ceremony - that she finally checked her personal phone.

    A short message had been waiting there since early morning. Blunt. And darkly appropriate. RIO: Like the dead.

    A soft scoff escaped her, followed by a thin, amused smile.

    She stared at the screen longer than necessary, wondering when exactly her life had begun to resemble a Scandinavian true-crime series.

    And more importantly, what kind of ending this one was quietly assembling behind her back. Chapter End Notes Sending so much love to all of you, my sweet and supportive readers. Thank you for sticking around.

    Every thoughtful comment and kudo means more than I can properly express. Truly. 🖤 (Happy New Year!)

    Chapter 23: Morally Purple Is My Favorite Color or The One

    Where Agatha Tries to Scrub Death Off Herself Chapter Summary A Completely "Reasonable" Response to Being Framed for Murder Chapter Notes Hello my little coven, Well.

    It's only been... (checks calendar, immediately regrets it) ...several months. In my defense, life happened, heartbreak happened, work happened, my brain happened, and at some point this chapter quietly expanded into one of those terrifying beasts that refuses to be finished until every sentence has been interrogated, rewritten, and audited. The good news is that we're sooooooo back.

    (Since it's been a while, I also took the opportunity to weave a few reminders and callbacks into the chapter itself. I know not everyone has time, or emotional stamina, to reread 150k+ words before a new update, so I tried to naturally bring back a few details that had only been mentioned much earlier in the story. Hopefully it makes jumping back into Unwritten a little easier.)

    See the end of the chapter for more notes Only after death had Dottie Jones (or whatever her actual name was) managed to become something she had never quite succeeded in being while alive: consequential. More importantly, she had succeeded, with a level of posthumous spite that deserved professional recognition, in becoming Agatha Harkness’s problem.

    The studio executive could already feel the damage propagating outward from that body in the woods, moving through her business like dye entering groundwater. Nothing in her world stayed contained at that scale. A corpse became scrutiny. And scrutiny had a habit of spreading.

    Eventually, it would reach everything she had spent years keeping carefully separated. And Agatha, who preferred outcomes arranged long before events ever reached the surface, despised problems she had not personally authorized in advance.

    The worst part was recognizing that she should have handled Dottie far more efficiently while circumstances still allowed it.

    The supermarket-scented performance of moral superiority had ceased being amusing months ago.

    She should have removed her. Erased the possibility of escalation before it ever became necessary.

    Instead, she had indulged herself. Circling the problem slowly, enjoying the pressure of it. Testing limits. Provoking reactions. Playing with her food instead of eliminating it cleanly. And now the consequences of her own arrogance were metastasizing faster than logistics could contain them.

    Once upon a time, she would have gone straight to securing the evidence, cracking the encryption hidden inside that absurd library card, uncovering whatever that contemptible excuse for a professional had buried inside Westview’s LTO archive had buried inside Westview’s LTO archive, redirecting suspicion, and quietly dismantling anyone reckless enough to stand in her way. She would have arrived at the evening premiere radiant, untouched by the machinery it took to get there. And afterward, as a reward for a productive day, she would still have found time to make some beautiful woman forget her own name before sunrise.

    But sometime over the past few months, the internal equations governing Agatha’s life had shifted. Or perhaps she had.

    Because this morning, instead of pursuing leverage or containing exposure or getting ahead of the disaster already spreading beneath her feet, she drove straight home. The encrypted card remained untouched in her coat pocket; whatever Dottie had hidden inside the archive stayed sealed, waiting for someone else to reach it first.

    Every hour widened the vulnerability. She knew that.

    And still, she drove home.

    For one simple reason: she wanted to be there before her son woke up. The older version of Agatha would have recognized the impulse as weakness. A structural flaw. The kind of sentimental compromise that got people killed.

    This version looked at her son’s sleeping certainty and found herself unable to care. She arrived just in time to catch that fragile in-between moment when sleep released him by degrees. Eyelashes fluttering, breathing shifting, that small bewildered frown children wore before memory returned.

    The moment Nicky saw her, the tension vanished from his face so completely it nearly split something open inside her chest.

    “Hey, kid”

    The smile that crossed Agatha’s face arrived instinctively, too fast to suppress. She leaned down, pressed a kiss against his temple, and brushed the sleep-tangled hair back from his forehead. Her hand lingered at his cheek a moment longer than necessary, as though touch itself might preserve the scene somehow. Hold it still a little longer before the rest of the world arrived demanding pieces of her again.

    Nicky leaned into the contact automatically. Trusting. Unthinking.

    She still had not adjusted to how natural that felt.

    Having him here still disoriented her. The quiet domesticity of it didn’t sit right. Caring for someone openly, and being cared for in return without suspicion or condition, felt almost unreal.

    “Morning, Mama” he mumbled, stretching out the word slightly, as though he still didn’t fully trust it not to disappear if he said it too quickly.

    Agatha understood that feeling intimately. She was still testing the sound of it herself. And when he smiled at her, crooked, warm, still halfway trapped inside sleep, she found herself memorizing the expression automatically with the ruthless attention of someone accustomed to losing beautiful things. Because happiness, in her experience, had always behaved like contraband. Temporary and confiscatable.

    “Hungry?” she asked softly, brushing the last traces of sleep from the corners of his eyes with her thumb.

    Nicky’s grin widened instantly.

    “Starving”

    He was always hungry.

    Not only for food. For routine, reassurance.

    He needed proof that tomorrow would resemble today. That breakfast would appear when promised. That people who said they were coming back actually would. He still hadn’t fully learned permanence yet. Hadn’t understood that love, when healthy, was not supposed to feel rented by the hour.

    Agatha recognized that hunger because once, long ago, it had hollowed her out from the inside too. That kind of absence taught people to expect loss before joy. She had built entire versions of herself around that expectation.

    Which was precisely why every unconscious way Nicky reached for her felt so pure and devastating.

    Because he still reached anyway.

    …

    They ate breakfast the way they had most mornings over the past few months: noisy, unhurried, comfortably familiar. The fact that it had become routine still struck Agatha as faintly miraculous.

    Nicky settled beside her instead of across the island, close enough that she could reach for him automatically between sips of coffee.

    “Hold still” she murmured, already gathering his hair.

    Naturally, he didn’t.

    He kept talking through toast, one knee bouncing against the cabinet beside her as an entire school crisis unraveled between bites. Apparently someone had committed fraud involving holographic trading cards, glue sticks, and offenses that escalated in severity every time he swallowed.

    The details shifted too quickly to fully follow.

    His mom listened anyway, attentively, strategically, with carefully rationed interjections. A question here. A quiet really? there. Just enough to keep the story moving. All while looping the elastic around his hair with the weary precision of someone performing the same minor correction to gravity every morning. Nicky liked his hair long. Maintaining it, however, held very little appeal. So every morning, without discussion, he eventually drifted toward her and allowed her to fix it.

    Eventually, as usual, excitement pulled him out of English and into the language that came first when he stopped thinking about it. It always happened when he stopped paying attention to himself. Words came faster then, brighter, less filtered. His hands became more animated, his face more expressive, speech slipping out before translation could catch up. Agatha followed most of it now. Not perfectly. But well enough to respond. Well enough to notice the small flash of delight whenever she did.

    She waited until he paused for breath before deliberately mangling a word. Nicky stopped dead.

    A tiny crease formed between his eyebrows.

    “No, no. You have to roll it more” The conversation vanished without ceremony. “Listen” He repeated the word slowly, patiently, with the solemn concentration of a deeply underpaid linguistics professor attempting to salvage the academic future of his worst student. Agatha repeated it back flawlessly.

    Nicky blinked.

    That reaction never got old.

    Long before he ever started calling her Mama, Agatha had decided language would not be allowed to stand between them.

    During those first supervised visits, his English arrived cautiously. Measured. Examined before release.

    Spanish was different. It escaped him. It was the language where laughter arrived first. Where his thoughts still moved faster than caution.

    And Agatha had no intention of losing access to any part of him simply because she lacked the vocabulary to follow him there.

    So she learned.

    At first she let him teach her whatever came naturally. Colors. Objects. Turning vocabulary into an excuse to spend a little longer together.

    Small shared territories disguised as lessons.

    What Nicky never realized was that after every visit, she went home and learned everything properly.

    Tutors.

    Audio lessons in traffic.

    Flashcards between meetings.

    Grammar exercises at two in the morning while exhaustion scraped against the inside of her skull.

    Because she had never tolerated obstacles gracefully. And this particular one stood between her and her son.

    By the time his English became effortless, as it inevitably would, her Spanish had no business being any good.

    Instead, she could now argue contracts, insult executives, and threaten producers fluently in two languages.

    But Nicky's version of events had long since settled into something much sweeter. In his mind, he had taught her everything. Every smooth conversation. Every perfectly rolled r. Every sentence she spoke belonged partially to him.

    The high-functioning disaster raising him had never corrected the misunderstanding. The illusion cost her nothing.

    Nicky's pride whenever she answered him in Spanish felt far too valuable to exchange for technical honesty.

    “Well,” she lifted her coffee with exaggerated dignity “I do happen to have an exceptional tutor.”

    “No, seriously” His expression softened into something earnest. “Your Spanish is really good now. Like… better than my teacher at school”

    Agatha snorted softly into her coffee.

    She had never transferred him after the adoption. Nicky had asked to stay exactly where he was, the same overcrowded public school he’d attended while ricocheting through the foster system, and Agatha, against every instinct favoring private institutions, had allowed i Emotional stability occasionally outweighed status and outranked elitism. That still didn’t stop her from having opinions.

    “That explains quite a lot about the California public school system” she muttered “Mama”

    “What?”

    He shook his head, already grinning. The crooked smile arrived a beat before the laughter did.

    “You sound really snobby when you talk like that”

    Agatha lifted an eyebrow over the rim of her cup.

    “Honey, I worked very hard to achieve this level of snobbery”

    That obliterated him.

    He folded, laughing hard enough to lose control of both his posture and the conversation. One hand slapped uselessly against the counter as he tried to breathe. And there it was again, that familiar tightening beneath her ribs.

    Agatha was used to making people laugh. She was simply not used to anyone finding her funny.

    Most laughter around her came with incentives. Careers. Favors. Survival instincts. In truth, she was rarely trying to be funny.

    Cutting, yes.

    Cruel, when necessary.

    Occasionally entertaining in the way controlled demolition could be entertaining from a safe distance.

    Nicky, however, seemed genuinely convinced she was hilarious.

    He never reacted to her like she was the terrifying Agatha Harkness. Never like she was the Reaper.

    To him, she was simply his mother saying ridiculous things over coffee. Somehow, that remained one of the most disorienting facts of her adult life. “Mama, you're crazy”

    Still laughing, he leaned sideways into her shoulder.

    The word landed with the same impossible force it always did.

    * Mama *

    Agatha suspected she could hear it every day for the rest of her life and never become accustomed to belonging to it.

    As she watched him stealing strawberries from her plate with the concentration of a tiny professional criminal, her thoughts drifted, inevitably, back to the exact moment her life had divided itself into a before and an after.

    The first time she met him.

    She remembered it with the unnatural clarity usually reserved for miracles, disasters, near- death experiences, exceptionally good kisses, and a handful of mistakes she would happily make again.

    Years ago, Westview had been sponsoring some foster initiative.

    The details no longer mattered.

    A building.

    A conference room.

    A collection of professionally compassionate adults congratulating one another for caring correctly.

    Agatha remembered none of their names.

    Only the door, slamming open hard enough to strike the wall. And the child who came flying through it.

    He couldn’t have been more than four. Small, breathless, moving too fast for the adults chasing him.

    She caught sight of scraped knees, untied sneakers, panic, before he crossed the room in a straight line and ducked behind her legs with the instinctive certainty of something that had found shelter without understanding why it had chosen it.

    Not Wanda.

    Not the director.

    Not the social worker.

    Agatha.

    Somehow, the child had looked at Agatha Harkness and mistaken her for safety. The thought still unsettled her. Even now. Especially now.

    A voice cut through the hallway moments later, exhausted, sharpened by the brittle authority of someone accustomed to obedience rather than trust. The kind of voice children learned to flinch from early.

    She looked down.

    The child looked up.

    Wide-eyed, shaking. Completely certain she could protect him.

    His fingers closed around the back of her blazer and stayed there.

    For one strange second, no one spoke.

    A staff member appeared in the doorway, breathless and already apologizing. Something about behavioral issues. Adjustment problems. Running off.

    She barely registered it, still too aware of the small weight pressed against her legs. Still aware that, despite every available alternative, the child had not let go. She could have stepped aside. One movement would have been enough. He would have been taken, returned to whatever had sent him running in the first place. She didn’t.

    The staff member stopped mid-step.

    Agatha never knew whether it was her expression that did it, or the delayed recognition of who she was.

    Either way, he stopped.

    People usually did.

    Whatever else the Reaper inspired in people, confidence was rarely part of it. She noticed, distantly, the uneasy glance exchanged between her then-fiancée, the staff member, and the director before the man quietly retreated into the hallway. Only then did she glance downward again.

    “And who do we have here?” The question emerged softer than anyone present had ever heard from her. “Think you can tell me your name, honey?”

    A small voice answered.

    And that was it.

    Nothing dramatic happened afterward. No cinematic revelation. No divine certainty descending from the heavens. No sudden clarity about fate or purpose. Just a frightened little boy saying his name without letting go of her blazer, as though she were the only stable thing left in the room.

    Looking back, that was probably the only part that mattered.

    Everything that followed, the lawyers, the interviews, the signatures, the bribes disguised as charitable donations, only formalized a decision already made.

    Administrative residue: paperwork and bureaucracy arriving long after the fact, trying to catch up with something they already knew.

    They were a family.

    Now he sat across from her, stealing strawberries from her plate while delivering an exhaustive analysis of some ridiculous goat simulator game with the grave intensity of a defense contractor briefing Congress.

    Real enough to reach for her food without asking. Comfortable enough to assume she would allow it. Safe enough to forget permission entirely.

    * Safe *

    The word felt different after that morning. Smaller. Less permanent than she had once believed.

    Nicky stole another strawberry.

    Agatha let him and watched him talk. Watched him exist.

    The gruesome events of that morning had reminded her how little stayed fixed for long. Lives shifted. Empires shifted. Stability was mostly a story people told themselves until reality became bored enough to interrupt.

    Every time Agatha let herself think seriously about leaving, something beneath her ribs tightened.

    The urge to stay was becoming a problem.

    Right now, the idea of canceling the flight altogether kept returning in slow, seductive waves. Let the body become somebody else's jurisdiction for a few hours and the missing files remain missing. Let the people circling her business sharpen their teeth without her immediate involvement for once.

    Stay here instead.

    Barefoot in her kitchen.

    Coffee cooling slowly between her hands while Nicky explained something utterly meaningless with the fierce concentration children reserved for subjects adults were apparently too stupid to appreciate properly.

    The fantasy felt dangerous.

    Worse. It felt reasonable.

    Agatha had survived too long by instinct not to recognize that particular kind of temptation. The moment she gave it coherent shape, it would begin asking things of her. And she had learned long ago that negotiating with herself was how disasters started. So she did what she always did with intolerable feelings.

    She redirected them into something smaller.

    Something survivable.

    A controlled act of irresponsibility.

    “Be honest” she said almost casually, stirring her coffee with absent elegance, like the thought just occurred to her “How necessary are we feeling school is today?” Nicky’s head snapped upward so quickly she briefly worried about his neck. “Wait” His eyes widened “Seriously?”

    Agatha hid a mischievous smile behind the rim of her mug.

    He already knew she was leaving later. She had told him before breakfast. Not for how long.

    She still hadn’t answered that part for herself.

    So he recognized the offer for what it was: something special disguised as spontaneity. A goodbye neither of them was willing to call one.

    "I'm thinking..." she set her mug down and gave a slow, thoughtful nod, pretending to weigh the options with great seriousness. "Beach day"

    Joy lit up his face with such uncomplicated intensity that it almost hurt to watch. He adored their beach days.

    At his age, he probably should have been drifting outward already. Leaning a little more toward classmates than home. Building a private world one harmless secret at a time. Beginning the long migration children eventually make toward lives that no longer orbit entirely around the people raising them.

    Her son had skipped that stage.

    Perhaps because nothing about the way they'd found each other had been ordinary enough to make distance feel safe.

    By the time they found each other, too much had already been lost. And afterward, life gave them remarkably little uninterrupted time to recover what remained. Most of their history existed in fragments instead of years: supervised visits, temporary routines, departures measured in countdowns rather than calendars.

    A few months of living together hadn't diluted his excitement over her existence. If anything, every separation sharpened it.

    Another breakfast across the kitchen island.

    Another evening sprawled together at opposite ends of the couch.

    Another perfectly forgettable Saturday transformed into something worth remembering simply because they happened to occupy it side by side.

    In Nicky's private cosmology, Agatha still occupied the center of the known universe. The person he wanted nearby whenever life became exciting, frightening, funny, confusing, or simply worth sharing.

    Which, translated into ordinary English, meant something wonderfully uncomplicated: His mama was the coolest person alive.

    To the ongoing horror of every joyless adult unfortunate enough to share a PTA mailing list with her, however, she was an institutional nightmare.

    Nicky's mother possessed the sort of charisma sensible people quietly classified as a public safety concern.

    Rules weakened around her. Authority lost structural integrity. Minor felonies acquired surprising educational value.

    Not because she encouraged recklessness. Because she made joy sound like a better argument.

    Around Agatha, the world briefly stopped behaving as though happiness always arrived attached to a receipt somebody would eventually demand to see.

    And that morning, she intended to earn every future complaint the PTA might someday file against her.

    She chose hot sand beneath bare feet and the boy sprinting toward her with soaked hands and criminal intent while she pretended, not especially convincingly, to escape. Melting ice cream running over both their wrists faster than either of them could eat it. And the profound satisfaction of helping him demolish an entire row of elaborately engineered sandcastles some optimistic architect had built far too close to the tide, the two of them reducing beachfront kingdoms to rubble with the solemn coordination of anarchists dismantling a monarchy.

    Nicky laughed until he stumbled. She laughed because he did.

    The world, astonishingly, survived two Harknesses behaving exactly as everyone had always warned it they would.

    Hours slipped past unnoticed. The tide erased every trace of their crimes without requiring apologies from either of them.

    Agatha would've called it a perfectly ordinary day. The kind respectable parents were probably discouraged from encouraging.

    Still...

    She suspected he'd remember it.

    Not because of the castles.

    Or the ice cream.

    Or the ocean.

    He'd remember that, for one entire morning, the world hadn't demanded that either of them behave.

    That happiness had been allowed to exist without anyone rushing to invoice it. And somewhere between collapsing kingdoms and melted vanilla, Agatha understood something she'd been avoiding for months: the dangerous thing wasn't loving this life. The dangerous thing was discovering she wanted to keep it.

    Whatever reality intended to charge her later...

    This had already been worth the bill.

    A few hours later, the beach had vanished so completely it might have belonged to someone else's life.

    Salt gave way to perfume.

    Sun-warmed skin disappeared beneath a tuxedo tailored exclusively for her. Where vanilla had dripped over her wrists that morning, diamonds now caught the light instead.

    Agatha Harkness™ was back.

    Money could purchase every piece she wore. It couldn't have taught anyone else how to inhabit it.

    She sat behind the wide black lacquer desk in her home office, one Louboutin hanging lazily from the tip of her foot while she worked through the last details demanding attention before the evening officially belonged to Hollywood again.

    In less than twelve hours she'd be several states away. Which, regrettably, required leaving her son behind.

    She understood the necessity. She still objected to it on principle. Hence why Nicky's deeply peculiar nanny was currently crouched beside her desk conducting what appeared to be a criminal investigation. One hand flattened against the floor. The other resting against the leg of the desk.

    "There"

    The desk moved. Barely. The sort of movement most people would've dismissed as imagination.

    "There what?"

    "Your desk wobbles"

    "It does not"

    The obnoxious employee pushed it.

    The desk shifted perhaps a millimeter.

    "It does"

    "So?"

    Agatha sighed.

    There were currently geopolitical situations receiving less scrutiny than this piece of furniture.

    "Hm" Yelena pushed again "It bothers me"

    Over the years Agatha had negotiated with senators, federal prosecutors, studio executives, hostile journalists, mad billionaires, and one deeply self-centered cult leader. None of them had ever pursued a point with Romanoff’ sister's level of commitment. The irritating part was that the blonde operative wasn't trying to be difficult. The desk genuinely bothered her.

    That sort of thing happened around her.

    Reality presented itself. Yelena noticed a detail nobody else cared about. The detail became her entire personality without delay.

    "Anyway" the strange young woman said, finally abandoning the floor and dropping into the chair opposite Agatha. "Continue"

    A moment later one leg was hooked over the armrest as though basic furniture etiquette had never been properly explained to her.

    The contrast between them was almost insulting.

    The impeccably dressed executive looked as though she belonged on the cover of a financial magazine.

    Yelena looked as though she belonged in an incident report: heavy boots, faded gray shirt, and a leather jacket that appeared to have survived several experiences better left undocumented.

    Nothing about her suggested childcare. Or patience. Or the routine responsibility of reminding someone to brush his teeth before bed.

    And she seemed entirely unburdened by the need to appear acceptable and treated authority less like a hierarchy and more like a rumor.

    None of it mattered.

    Natasha had vouched for her.

    Months earlier, when Agatha had asked Westview Productions' Head of Security why she should trust her son's safety to her younger sister, Romanoff hadn't offered a résumé or listed qualifications. She'd simply looked up from whatever report occupied her attention at the time and said: "Death itself would have trouble getting past Yelena"

    And, after a pause long enough to suggest she considered the second point equally important, she added: "Also she's weirdly good with kids"

    At the time, Agatha had considered both claims equally improbable.

    Experience had been forced to intervene.

    The residential field agent had entered their lives gradually. An evening here. A weekend there. The occasional overnight stay when the studio head had work or…other commitments. Nicky adapted first.

    That wasn't surprising.

    He responded to consistency more readily than charm, he cared about consistency. Yelena never became a different version of herself depending on who happened to be in the room, and Nicky trusted that instinctively. And he adored her.

    The more unexpected discovery was that the feeling appeared to be mutual. Yelena remembered things nobody had asked her to remember.

    The teacher Nicky avoided.

    The cereal he denied liking while finishing the entire box.

    The difference between ordinary boredom and the particular silence that meant something was wrong.

    She paid attention once. After that she simply behaved accordingly. Without ever asking to be thanked for it. Just competence.

    Agatha knew what would happen while she was gone.

    Nicky would be fed. The apartment would be checked before bed. If something felt wrong, Yelena would notice long before anyone else did. She would check the locks. Check the windows. Pause whenever the building made a sound she didn't recognize. She would get up if Nicky called out during the night. She would notice if something was wrong and she would respond by whatever became necessary.

    The woman currently folded into one of Agatha's Herman Miller chairs in a position fundamentally incompatible with both ergonomics and basic human anatomy looked deeply unsuited to domestic life, yet she was observant, resourceful, fiercely protective of her son, and alarmingly capable of turning ordinary household objects into improvised weapons. Rationally, there was nothing more to prepare.

    But motherhood had proven remarkably indifferent to reason.

    Before Nicky, risk had been something Agatha calculated. Preparation eliminated most of it. Experience eliminated the rest.

    Then she became responsible for someone she could not afford to lose. Now every solution seemed to generate another possibility she hadn't considered yet. Every precaution uncovered another scenario waiting just beyond it.

    She hadn't become irrational. She had simply acquired infinitely more ways to imagine losing everything.

    The two women regarded each other across the office.

    Agatha sighed.

    The entire situation remained absurd.

    "If he has a nightmare..."

    "He won't." Yelena crossed one boot over the opposite knee. "Statistically" Her boss arched a brow.

    "That's not how statistics work"

    "Fine." A shrug "Then he has a nightmare. He survives the nightmare. Problem solved" Patience, Agatha reminded herself as she pinched her nose, remained considerably cheaper than (another) murder.

    "If he does have one, he likes water"

    "I know"

    "He sleeps better if…"

    "Bathroom light stays on" Yelena replied, still staring at the allegedly defective desk. Agatha tried again.

    "Remember, he pretends he isn't sick until approximately…"

    "Thirty seconds before he throws up"

    The ex-spy picked up a crystal paperweight and began tossing it lazily from one hand to the other.

    "I know that too”

    Silence.

    Then: "You know I know"

    * Yes. Of course she knew. That wasn't the point. *

    The paperweight rose.

    Fell.

    Rose again.

    Caught without effort.

    It had cost nearly two thousand dollars. The woman currently responsible for Nicky's continued existence handled it like it had come free with a children's meal. The last of the evening sunlight flashed briefly through the crystal each time it spun. "And if someone comes sniffing around?" Agatha asked.

    The paperweight stopped.

    That was the question.

    Not nightmares.

    Not stomach bugs.

    Not bedtime routines.

    This.

    The corner of the nanny's mouth twitched.

    "I tell them to go fuck themselves"

    Agatha might have pinched the bridge of her nose if she hadn't already been doing exactly that.

    "Professionalism"

    "What?"

    "Try it"

    The former mercenary considered the suggestion.

    "I relocate Nicky”

    A pause.

    "I call you"

    She nodded once, apparently satisfied with her own reasoning.

    "Then I tell them to go fuck themselves"

    Despite herself, the worried mother laughed.

    A mistake.

    Positive reinforcement only encouraged the younger Romanoff's natural tendency toward unfiltered commentary. (Not that Agatha was entirely convinced Romanoff belonged on either sister's birth certificate).

    "You’re just getting in your head"

    The media mogul folded her arms, deeply committed to her own indignation “The situation is serious"

    "Every situation is serious"

    The paperweight finally returned to the desk. Not where it belonged, but where it functioned as a remarkably expensive shim. Agatha strongly suspected that had been Yelena's objective from the beginning.

    "You think I do not understand"

    "I know you don't"

    However good the enemy of unstable furniture was at her job, she was still operating without the full picture. Then again, so was everybody else.

    “So what?”

    The eccentric babysitter stared at her for a long second. Long enough to make Agatha wonder whether she understood considerably more than she ever admitted.

    "Everybody thinks their story is special"

    A finger pointed at her own chest.

    "Mine"

    Then at Agatha.

    "Yours"

    Toward the hallway.

    "Mailman's"

    A shrug.

    "Details change"

    Without warning, she spun once in the chair.

    A complete revolution.

    The chair stopped exactly where it had started.

    Yelena looked back at Agatha with absolute seriousness, as though nothing unusual had happened.

    "Job stays the same"

    She tapped her own chest again.

    "I protect the kid"
