    That objective description of responsibilities should not have been reassuring. Somehow it was.

    “Fine by me”

    She studied the eccentric Russian woman for a moment before adding: "One more thing"

    Yelena looked suspicious.

    "As far as he's concerned, nothing is wrong"

    For the first time all evening, the sitter stopped moving.

    "Oh" The single syllable landed differently than the others. "You want him to stay a kid" "As long as possible"

    "I can do that" Yelena nodded. “I can keep the fairytale alive”

    Something inside Agatha loosened.

    Inevitably, the nanny ruined it.

    "It'll be okay"

    The protective mother almost argued.

    The words arrived unsupported by evidence, probability, or anything else she normally trusted.

    "You don't know that”

    "No" the shadow assigned to her boy settled deeper into the chair "But it has to be" The answer should have sounded naïve. Instead it landed with the stubborn weight of something that had already survived disappointment.

    For once, Yelena wasn't joking. Wasn't provoking or pretending not to care. She simply believed the alternative was unacceptable.

    "Yeah" Agatha said quietly. "It has to be"

    The self-appointed furniture auditor suddenly looked away. Toward the windows. The city. Anywhere except her boss.

    As though she'd accidentally revealed more than intended.

    Agatha simply watched her.

    * Maybe Natasha had been far too modest when describing her sister * A soft knock sounded.

    The office door drifted inward a few inches.

    It hadn't closed properly in months.

    Children altered architecture in unexpected ways. Walls remained where they had always been. Locks continued to function. Yet every room somehow became easier to enter once they belonged to someone small enough to ignore boundaries as a matter of principle. "I took, like, twenty pictures."

    Nicky's voice arrived before he did.

    A giant purple calla lily appeared in the doorway.

    For several seconds, that was all anyone saw.

    Then a dinosaur-print pajama leg emerged beneath it.

    Followed by fleeting glimpses of brown hair as Nicky maneuvered the plant through the doorway with the solemn concentration of someone transporting unstable nuclear material. Whatever conversation had occupied the room quietly surrendered.

    "Most of them were blurry, though."

    The flower advanced farther into the office.

    Presumably Nicky was somewhere behind it.

    Eventually enough of him became visible to confirm that the lily had not, in fact, achieved independent locomotion.

    Earlier, Agatha had needed twenty uninterrupted minutes with the nanny. Inside her household, that much uninterrupted time generally required a carefully engineered distraction.

    Today's version involved handing Nicky her phone and suggesting he photograph the calla lily somewhere with better lighting.

    It was a transparently ridiculous excuse.

    The lily normally lived on the corner of her desk in the brightest room of the penthouse, a practical arrangement born from Agatha's stubborn refusal to wear reading glasses unless absolutely necessary. She preferred to conduct meetings with her dignity intact rather than squint at documents like a haunted Victorian medium deciphering cursed letters by candlelight.

    Neither of them had pretended to believe the lighting was the real reason. Least of all Nicky.

    Fortunately, he possessed an almost limitless enthusiasm for cameras, buttons, and anything that even vaguely resembled artistic experimentation.

    Especially when he suspected the adults were being weird.

    So he'd accepted the assignment anyway.

    Now, with a small grunt of effort, Nicky hoisted the pot onto what had become the most discussed piece of furniture in the house.

    "Scratchy wouldn't stop trying to eat it."

    "Nicholas." "That plant is toxic." The warning arrived simultaneously.

    Nicky stopped moving.

    His gaze bounced from Agatha to Yelena and back again. A quick assessment of available allies.

    The results were discouraging.

    "Okay, wow" He frowned. "That's a lot of judgement"

    Once again, Agatha felt a brief and deeply unpleasant sensation of recognition. The expression.

    The tone.

    The theatrical indignation.

    At some point her son had apparently begun borrowing pieces of her personality without requesting permission first.

    Which, in retrospect, was probably how parenthood worked.

    You spent years teaching a small human how to function. Then one day they folded their arms, objected to authority, and sounded exactly like you.

    He sighed the way only children and pets could sigh, like someone carrying an unreasonable burden imposed by a fundamentally disappointing society.

    Neither woman seemed particularly moved by it.

    Yelena reached over and ruffled his hair. Nicky accepted the gesture with the tolerance normally reserved for eccentric relatives.

    Sensing that the discussion about poisonous plants was unlikely to improve his evening, he abandoned the subject entirely and shifted his attention toward safer territory: flattery. He looked at Agatha. At the version of his mother that only seemed to exist on certain nights. The smile appeared first. The one that had already negotiated its way out of consequences more than once.

    "You look fancy"

    He turned toward Yelena. Seeking confirmation. Or ammunition. Possibly both. "She looks fancy, right?"

    His accomplice studied the boss lady with unexpected seriousness.

    The tuxedo.

    The diamonds.

    The hair.

    The watch.

    The expression currently informing them that patience was a finite resource. "Da" The verdict arrived after due consideration. “Like crow”

    “A crow?” Nicky spread his arms and gave them an indignant flap.

    Yelena nodded.

    “Very expensive crow, yes"

    He turned back toward his mother looking delighted. The clarification seemed to improve the comparison considerably.

    Agatha briefly considered disowning him. Instead, she rested an elbow on the desk and pressed two fingers against her temple.

    The former mercenary saw the gesture and understood it instantly. She rose before anyone managed to say another word.

    "Macaroni for dinner?"

    A distraction. A shamelessly obvious distraction.

    The effect on Nicky was immediate. His attention abandoned the crow comparison. "Duh. Mac and cheese is perfect food"

    "Based on what research?" his worried mom asked.

    Nutritionally speaking, the dish occupied a narrow strip of territory somewhere between wishful thinking and negligence.

    Then again, Agatha hadn't hired Yelena for her nutritional expertise. "Science!" Nicky and his irresponsible nanny announced in perfect unison. Before Agatha could object, they launched into whatever deeply suspicious handshake had apparently developed behind her back.

    Finger tap.

    Wrist turn.

    Knuckle collision.

    A final snap.

    Executed with the ease of something repeated often enough to stop requiring conscious thought.

    She watched in silence.

    At some point an entire language had developed in her peripheral vision and neither participant appeared interested in translating.

    Yelena turned toward the door.

    Halfway there, she stopped.

    "Open or closed?"

    "Closed"

    That anti-authoritarian nanny nodded thoughtfully. Then left it open. Naturally. Footsteps faded down the hallway.

    Soon came the sounds of kitchen activity: cabinet doors, drawers, the metallic collision of cookware being moved around with questionable enthusiasm.

    A few seconds later, her voice drifted back toward the office.

    "Do not annoy your mother too much"

    The rattle of something stainless steel.

    "Or no macaroni"

    Nicky snorted and laughed so hard he nearly folded in half.

    Agatha turned slowly in her chair. One eyebrow climbed upward.

    "Well?"

    The laughter disappeared because he recognized the tone.

    "I kept moving him away"

    "Mm"

    "Every time"

    "Mm"

    "But he kept coming back"

    She reached for the flower and examined it with noticeably more concern than she had shown Dottie Jones's corpse that morning.

    One lifted leaf.

    A careful turn of the pot.

    Another leaf.

    No bite marks.

    No torn edges.

    No damaged stems.

    No evidence that Scratchy had recently attempted suicide through horticulture. "You are absolutely certain he didn't chew on it?"

    He pressed a hand dramatically against his chest.

    "Mami, I'd never let Scratchy poison himself"

    The outrage in his voice suggested she had accused him of a felony rather than a reasonable question about animal instincts.

    But a lifetime spent preparing for worst-case scenarios did not disappear simply because a small boy had mastered the tactical use of the word mami. So Agatha examined the lily anyway.

    The final inspection confirmed the complete absence of rabbit-related crimes. Only then did something in her shoulders loosen.

    "Alright" She released the leaf. "I believe you"

    Seemingly satisfied with the verdict, Nicky circled the desk and stopped beside her chair. Without a word, he reached over and gently straightened a petal that had twisted during his mother’s inspection.

    "Besides, I know you'd be really sad if something happened to this one" Agatha turned slowly.

    "Would I?"

    "Yeah” he rolled his eyes “You loooove it."

    The word stretched into something both theatrical and deeply annoying, in the uniquely gifted way only children seemed capable of when making utterly outrageous and ridiculous declarations.

    "I beg your pardon?"

    The question emerged wrapped in that old-Hollywood cadence Agatha instinctively retreated into whenever she felt emotionally cornered and fully intended to deny everything. Nicky ignored the performance entirely. He just stared at her.

    "I think it's helping"

    "Helping with what?"

    "Your..."

    His brow furrowed. One hand made an impatient circle in the air while he searched for the phrase.

    Agatha could practically watch him digging through his vocabulary.

    Suddenly his eyes widened.

    "Your black thumb"

    "My what?"

    "You know" He grinned, delighted with himself. "Like the opposite of a green thumb" "Is this botanical slander?"

    "Remember the cactus?" Nicky lowered his thumb like a Roman emperor delivering judgment. "That thing never stood a chance"

    Agatha scoffed, now completely sure that she was, in fact, raising a smaller, significantly less emotionally repressed version of herself.

    "That cactus died because its time had come"

    The look her son gave her carried the weary disappointment of someone forced to supervise a repeat offender.

    "Mama, please"

    "It lived a full life"

    "It was three months old"

    "A full and meaningful life"

    "You said that about the orchid"

    "No" she sat up straighter "I said orchids are manipulative little things" "They're flowers."

    "Exactly"

    "I don't think that means anything."

    "It means everything, hon"

    Nicky looked at her for another second before asking: "And the rosemary?"

    She chose not to comment on the rosemary because the historical record was not entirely on her side.

    Plant life had rarely experienced measurable success around Agatha Harkness. Things arrived in her home vibrant, optimistic, and biologically committed to survival. Then, gradually, they seemed to reconsider: Mint blackened mysteriously. Basil collapsed under mysterious circumstances. One aloe plant had simply liquefied without explanation. The rosemary bush remained her favorite incident. It had died with such abrupt theatricality she still suspected personal resentment.

    The cactus, however, remained the low point.

    Nature had spent millions of years engineering the thing specifically for neglect. Harsh climates. Minimal water. Entire ecosystems built around the assumption that nothing could accidentally kill it.

    Agatha had still managed to do exactly that in record time.

    And yet the ridiculous lily continued behaving as though the rules governing every other plant simply did not apply.

    It survived.

    More annoyingly, it flourished.

    Each week brought new blooms, dark petals unfolding with the quiet self-possession of something already certain of its future.

    That was the offensive part. Not the survival per se. The confidence. The flower behaved as though the matter had already been decided. As though it belonged there. And Agatha would continue watering it, turning it toward the light, and making room for whatever it chose to become.

    Somewhere along the way, the ridiculous flower had stopped feeling temporary. Like far too many things in Agatha's life lately.

    A life full of routines and expectations, where she was no longer alone. A life where things depended on her, expected her, counted on her.

    Where she worried about whether a rabbit had eaten something poisonous. Whether a child would have nightmares while she was gone.

    And where she cared far too much about a beautiful, infuriatingly high-maintenance, dark- eyed…

    * Plant *

    Beside her, the junior Harkness was still studying the lily too.

    After a moment, he glanced at her and blurted: "I'm really proud of you"

    The words landed a full second late. Not only because they were unexpected. Because they were hers.

    The exact phrase she gave him after difficult mornings. After good report cards. After frustrations swallowed instead of launched across rooms. And hard conversations survived instead of avoided. Small victories she treated like miracles because there had been a time when simply making it through the day had gone uncelebrated.

    And now he was handing the words back to her. Like they belonged there and they were simply…true.

    "You are?" she asked softly.

    He shrugged, looking almost embarrassed by having said it.

    "Yeah"

    And somehow that simple answer left her momentarily without a response. Fortunately, Nicky's attention span intervened before she had to acknowledge it. "Oh" He dug into the pocket of his dinosaur pajama pants. "The pictures came out really good"

    A second later he produced Agatha's phone.

    "You should post some"

    Immediately suspicious, his mother held out her hand.

    "Absolutely not"

    “I’m just saying”

    The grin that appeared instantly told her everything she needed to know. Several weeks earlier, a nearly identical expression had preceded the unauthorized publication of a video featuring Scratchy eating dried apples on her carefully curated Instagram account. The incident ended with a lengthy lecture involving privacy, public image, digital footprints, and why social-media managers eventually developed substance- abuse problems.

    Back then Nicky had appeared genuinely remorseful…for almost eight minutes. Now he stood there with her phone extended between them, wiggling his eyebrows at her with theatrical enthusiasm.

    "People should know"

    "Know what?"

    He gestured toward the flower as though it were all the proof anyone could possibly need. "That you finally kept one alive"

    "Nicholas" Agatha flexed the fingers of her outstretched hand. "Phone" This time he surrendered it.

    Well.

    Almost.

    Before she could close her hand around the device, he carefully lowered it onto her palm and trapped it there beneath both of his.

    "Promise me you won't look at them now"

    Agatha gave him a very specific look. The maternal equivalent of a subpoena. Her sweet prince lasted approximately three seconds before cracking. "They're for later"

    "Later?"

    "When you're gone"

    "Ah"

    Her expression softened despite herself.

    "I wanted you to have very cool ones"

    “Why?”

    He looked at his feet "So you can do your thing "

    "What thing?"

    “You know” he shrugged again. "Looking at pictures when you miss us" Agatha looked at the deeply suspicious little gremlin currently conducting an unauthorized audit of her personality.

    There should have been regulations governing this. Oversight. Certification requirements. Something. Children were not supposed to notice this much.

    "So when I eventually look through these" she said, setting the phone beside her laptop "I'm going to discover Scratchy was cast in this production?"

    Nicky suddenly found something fascinating over her shoulder.

    "Maybe"

    Agatha looked at him and shook her head in mock disapproval.

    * Children. They were exhausting *

    He wasn’t wrong, though.

    Somewhere halfway across the country, in a hotel room designed to convince wealthy people that loneliness was a meaningful experience, she probably would end up scrolling through those photographs.

    Still, that wasn't the real reason she'd asked him to photograph the lily. Some arguments were easier to win with evidence than with words. Especially when the audience consisted of the most stubborn woman she'd ever known.

    The phone had barely touched the desk before it vibrated.

    She glanced at the screen once and flipped it face-down.

    "Work?" her tiny traitor asked.

    By now, he understood that almost every interruption reaching his mother belonged, in one way or another, to work.

    "Worse" She slid the phone aside. "Aunt Lilia"

    That earned her another burst of laughter. Bright, helpless, entirely too delighted by her baseline cynicism.

    She watched him for a moment, faintly concerned. There was something vaguely alarming about how naturally Nicky had begun finding her dysfunction entertaining. Perhaps that was how corruption actually reproduced itself. Not through grand moral collapse, but through accumulation. Spend enough time raising a child and eventually even your coping mechanisms started installing themselves inside him like inherited software bugs.

    From somewhere down the hall came Yelena's voice.

    "Macaroni is ready. Also very tasty"

    Mother and son exchanged a look. A brief moment of perfect mutual understanding. This was about to become normal.

    When Agatha had explained he would be spending the next several days with the nanny, Nicky had simply nodded and accepted it.

    He had not bargained or attempted to negotiate additional privileges. He hadn't even invented sudden emergencies requiring immediate maternal attention.

    Children who expected people to come back usually protested a little. They were supposed to stall.

    Nicky adapted instead.

    That didn’t make the departure easier.

    The phone vibrated again against the desk.

    Ignoring it completely, she rose from the chair, slipped it into her pocket, and opened one arm.

    "Come here, hon"

    The room shifted around the invitation.

    Goodbye had entered it.

    Nicky moved toward her, arms already opening and she gathered him close, one hand settling at the back of his head.

    For a moment, nothing beyond the apartment seemed capable of reaching her. Not the premiere waiting downtown, not the operation already unfolding without her, not even the body lying in the woods.

    Only him.

    "You and me, darling"

    "You and me, Mama"

    The familiar refrain. Repeated often enough that neither remembered when it had stopped being a phrase and become a promise.

    She held him longer than necessary.

    Five selfish seconds.

    Maybe ten.

    Long enough to start taking inventory: The warmth still lingering in his skin from the sun; the uneven rhythm of breathing not entirely recovered from laughter; the exact weight of him leaning against her.

    She stored each detail carefully, the way other people stored valuables before a storm, or provisions before winter.

    Because she still didn't know how long she would be gone. Days, if everything behaved. Which meant weeks, almost certainly.

    When they finally separated, Nicky kissed her cheek and headed toward the hallway. Halfway there, he stopped.

    His mother watched realization arrive: the pause, the small furrow between his brows, the certainty that something remained unfinished.

    He turned around, crossed the room in three determined strides, reached up, and kissed her cheek again.

    More deliberately this time. As though the first goodbye had required revision. Agatha stood perfectly still, momentarily defenseless.Outmaneuvered by a child in dinosaur pajama shorts.

    That one she kept too.

    His footsteps faded down the hall.

    Silence returned.

    Not the old kind.

    The apartment had stopped feeling empty the day the boy she'd kill for moved in. The phone vibrated again.

    Agatha closed her eyes briefly before pulling it from her pocket.

    A voice note.

    She regarded the notification with immediate suspicion.

    Still, a voice note from the only oracle she tolerated was preferable to a phone call. Voice notes could be paused. Lilia could not.

    So naturally, against her better judgment and entirely in accordance with her actual personality, she pressed play.

    The House’s voice emerged low and distant, touched by that peculiar cadence she occasionally slipped into when she no longer sounded entirely anchored to the present. As though she were speaking from somewhere very far away.

    The bottom of a well.

    The far side of a prophecy.

    Or worse..from experience.

    "I thought she was the Tower upright, Agatha. I was wrong”

    A breath.

    “Listen to me. She's not the path forward."

    "What?"

    The word escaped before she could stop it.

    Silence answered. Several long seconds of it. Until her best frenemy spoke again, still wrapped in that eerie half-trance that always made her sound distant and unsettlingly certain at the same time.

    "Something terrible follows this. Disaster. Destruction. Sudden upheaval." The message ended.

    Agatha lowered the phone slowly.

    The problem wasn't that Lilia spoke in riddles. She always had.

    What bothered her was the shift beneath them.

    Lately, Lilia seemed less interested in the disaster itself than in Agatha's place within it. As though the future mattered less than the woman walking toward it.

    That was new.

    And deeply irritating.

    Her oldest critic no longer sounded like someone reading fate.

    She sounded like someone reading her.

    Not her circumstances. Not the crisis of the week.

    Her.

    The choices she kept making. The roads she insisted were different despite leading to the same destination. The stubborn certainty that this time she understood the risks well enough to survive them.

    Lilia saw the pattern now.

    And Agatha, whose ego required its own zip code, hated that, because somehow it felt far more invasive than prophecy.

    To be understood implied a kind of exposure. And Lilia had become alarmingly good at both. Which was precisely why she had ignored every attempt to reach her since leaving the woods.

    She was tired of warnings. Tired of conversations that always found their way back to the same conclusion, no matter where they started.

    Besides, as the undisputed CEO of delusional pragmatism, she remained firmly convinced that avoidance counted as emotional regulation if practiced with sufficient discipline. She intended to defend that position until reality managed to assemble a convincing counterargument.

    So when the phone vibrated again with another message from her increasingly inconvenient oracle, Agatha gave the screen exactly one second of consideration before locking it and dropping it into the evening bag that had spent the afternoon hanging from the back of her chair and now rested looped around her wrist. And leave.

    A problem temporarily unseen remained, in her opinion, a problem displaying admirable manners.

    The mirror in the hallway caught her on the way out.

    She stopped and studied her reflection for a moment.

    Pure vanity.

    * Mirrors existed for a reason, right? *

    The reflection offered no objections. The tuxedo remained flawless, the lace beneath it exactly where she wanted it.

    Makeup intact.

    Not even her hair had betrayed her.

    The deeply self-satisfied producer regarded her reflection for another second before arriving at the only reasonable conclusion: Against all available evidence, perfection appeared to be holding up remarkably well.

    She continued downstairs.

    Despite her resident prophet of doom's increasingly unsettling accuracy, one thing had never changed.

    Her prophecies had yet to alter Agatha's behavior.

    If anything, they mostly resulted in temporary no-contact policies.

    Tonight wasn't likely to break the tradition.

    What awaited her next couldn't be solved by prophecy.

    It required Wanda’s cooperation.

    And the ginger menace had never shown the slightest interest in making her ex fiancée’s life simpler.

    Quite the opposite.

    She possessed a remarkable talent for taking situations that were merely complicated and committing to them with frightening permanence.

    That, too, was a pattern.

    Los Angeles changed character once the sun slipped behind the hills. Glass towers lingered in the last light, holding gold along their edges long after the sky had surrendered it. Storefronts brightened beneath the palms. People emerged from tinted cars already wearing the versions of themselves intended for public consumption. Usually, Agatha found the performance comforting.

    A city built on reinvention understood certain courtesies. No one expected sincerity and no one asked questions they didn't want answered.

    Tonight, however, the artificiality only sharpened her awareness of how many directions her life had begun collapsing in at once.

    Traffic thickened around her in ribbons of red and white as she moved through it one-handed, steering with absent confidence while the glow of a burner phone illuminated her other palm. Offshore accounts appeared and vanished beneath her fingertips.

    Transfers authorized.

    Problems redistributed.

    Damage postponed rather than solved.

    Meanwhile, her legitimate phone lay face-up in the passenger seat, lighting every few seconds with the stubborn rhythm of obligations refusing neglect.

    Herbert, almost certainly.

    His messages would be impeccably phrased. Professional concern wrapped around increasingly urgent problems. The language of an assistant forced to manage consequences created by someone too important to blame openly.

    Her personal phone was worse.

    Buried somewhere inside the small black purse tossed across the back seat, it had spent the drive vibrating beneath lipstick, folded cash, that fake overdue library card, and a loaded handgun.

    An inventory that felt, in retrospect, uncomfortably representative of her priorities. Three phones.

    Three lives.

    Three carefully maintained fictions.

    All demanding something.

    And, as though that wasn’t already enough, Wanda had somehow managed to make her late. What should've been a brisk negotiation had expanded into the better part of an afternoon. Remarkably, they hadn't fought.

    No raised voices.

    No shattered glasses.

    No spectacular emotional bloodshed.

    Most remarkably of all, neither of them had mentioned that night.

    Or the months Agatha had simply...ghosted her.

    Somehow, that proved far more exhausting than another argument would've been. Her nightmare of a woman possessed an almost supernatural talent for making silence feel inhabited. Entire conversations unfolded inside the things she deliberately chose not to say, until omission itself acquired the weight of another person sitting between them. So Agatha filled the silence herself.

    The body.

    The investigation.

    The investigation.

    S.H.I.E.L.D.

    Westview.

    Wanda listened. Tea cooling between her hands. Green eyes fixed on the Queen of Lies with that unsettling degree of concentration that always felt less like concern than analysis. Agatha knew the expression.

    Her ex was sorting, keeping, discarding. Following every loose thread backward until she reached the hand that had tied the knot.

    And she already knew where that opportunist had arrived.

    Nicky was a vulnerability.

    Everything else was weather.

    The corpse, the federal attention, the empire threatening to buckle beneath simultaneous pressure. Those were merely the costumes fear happened to be wearing today. The thing underneath remained embarrassingly simple: Agatha was afraid for her son. And the opportunist she'd been stupid enough to almost marry, naturally, had seen it. Motherhood and loss had altered that manipulative little shit in ways Agatha still struggled to articulate.

    People liked to romanticize suffering. They talked about healing. Perspective. Softness. As though grief naturally enlarged a person.

    Wanda seemed to have undergone the opposite transformation. They had distilled her. Life had burned away every unnecessary hesitation until only instinct remained. Fear became a language she recognized in other people because she carried enough of her own. She saw through the woman who brought problems to her doorstep at once: that kid was the only genuine pressure point Agatha Harkness possessed.

    Leverage.

    For the first time in years, the woman who billed chaos by the hour had found herself negotiating from a position her opponent understood instinctively.

    Months ago, Wanda might have disguised that realization beneath sympathy. Or charm. Or the performance respectable women gave one another before negotiating something ugly. These days she seemed to regard decorum as an unnecessary expense so she allowed the silence to breathe. Long enough for anyone who didn't know her to believe she was still deciding.

    Agatha, who knew better, watched that sociopath’s fingertips resting lightly against the side of her mug as her gaze drifted toward the grain of the coffee table. And knew exactly what was happening.

    That ambitious little snake wasn't deciding whether to help. That decision had been made before Agatha finished explaining the situation. She was deciding what became possible now. "Okay" The sigh that followed belonged on a stage. "Fine"

    Wanda lifted her mug, took a slow sip, and finally pronounced sentence with all the martyrdom of a woman reluctantly agreeing to carry civilization on her own shoulders. "I'll take out your trash for you, you gorgeous hypocrite"

    The words should have sounded playful. Instead they arrived wrapped inside an unsettling tone Agatha hadn't heard in years.

    She knew that voice, long before prestige campaigns, photographed philanthropy and expensive respectability. Back when both of them were still climbing through the lower floors of Westview Productions, sleeping very little, lying professionally, and discovering that power usually introduced itself through ugly people in ugly places.

    Back when Wanda still worked alongside that miserable little cult called H.Y.D.R.A. Agatha had never cared much for the organization itself. The ideology was embarrassingly rigid. The methods lacked imagination. But she’d understood quickly what fascinated her then partner about them: their talent for transforming violence into inevitability, and their ability to make destruction sound reasonable.

    Then Pietro died.

    She never learned exactly what had happened after Pietro died. Wanda certainly never explained it. She only remembered the aftermath.

    Phones stopped ringing. Doors that had always opened simply... didn't anymore. Lives contracted with such methodical precision that by the time most people realized something was wrong, there was almost nothing left to recover. Eventually, bodies followed. Through all of it, Miss Good Publicity had sounded exactly the same. Soft and affectionate. Agatha found herself smirking despite everything. That voice was the entire reason she'd driven across Los Angeles to that aggressively suburban wasteland.

    She hadn't gone looking for a reasonable woman. Reasonable women recommended therapy. They believed in proportional responses, and entertained the adorable fiction that time improved difficult situations.

    Oh, no.

    She had needed the Scarlet Bitch.

    The possessive psychopath whose imagination treated murder as little more than an intellectual exercise and whose favorite contradiction remained introducing her ex partner as her ex-best friend while behaving as though Agatha herself still belonged under her jurisdiction. Her responsibility.

    She knew feeding Wanda's obsession was spectacularly irresponsible. But circumstances had developed a distressing habit of rewarding bad ideas.

    Elektra's photographs had answered one inconvenient question.

    S.H.I.E.L.D. had stopped merely observing Wanda.

    They were courting her. Testing the ground. Looking for a way in.

    The solution offended her by how obvious it was: Keep Hollywood’s favorite widow too busy protecting Westview to start entertaining their attention.

    The studio had always been Wanda’s favorite toy anyway. She loved the meetings, the events, the endless choreography required to convince the world that her ideas and products were the best.

    Fine.

    Let her have it. For now.

    Once The Witch installed herself at the front of Westview, S.H.I.E.L.D. would have to go through her first.

    So would everyone else.

    And Los Angeles hadn’t forgotten what it meant when Harkness and Maximoff stopped competing and started agreeing.

    One inconvenient woman.

    Two unrelated problems.

    Agatha appreciated that kind of arithmetic.

    Even when it required pretending to compromise.

    She handed Wanda exactly what the world believed power looked like.

    Her old position as Head of Creative Development.

    Her old office.

    The board meetings.

    The premieres.

    The interviews.

    Every polished surface respectable enough to survive magazine profiles and shareholder reports.

    The timing could even be marketed as generosity.

    The grieving widow returning to work.

    A celebrated executive reclaiming the position she'd never truly stopped belonging in. Hollywood adored a comeback almost as much as it adored a tragedy.

    Naturally, Wanda wanted everything.

    Agatha even agreed to stand beside her that evening, smiling for photographers as though continuity weren't simply another product Westview happened to manufacture particularly well.

    Everything beneath that façade stayed exactly where it had always been. Untouched.

    Invisible.

    Wanda had been given the storefront.

    Never the vault.

    From the outside, it would look remarkably like trust.

    Agatha knew better.

    Whether that loose cannon still remembered the difference remained an altogether separate problem.

    One she'd deal with after she came home.

    The premiere had already begun several floors above her by the time she pulled into the underground garage beneath the theater.

    The engine died.

    Silence rushed in after it.

    Abrupt.

    Almost hostile.

    Agatha didn't move.

    She sat with both hands resting on the steering wheel while cooling metal ticked softly around her. Then she folded forward, forehead against the leather, until something halfway between a laugh and a groan escaped her throat.

    She had spent the entire day refusing to come apart.

    Eventually, her mind simply ran out of ways to postpone it.

    After too many hours without nicotine or sleep, she was beginning to suspect there might, in fact, be such a thing as girlbossing too hard.

    * Fuck death *

    Well.

    Not death itself.

    Deaths happened.

    People like her learned early to account for bodies the same way legitimate industries accounted for taxes, and market fluctuations.

    Corpses were rarely the true complication.

    * Fuck Evanora *

    There it was.

    The name she'd spent the entire day (and most of her adult life) refusing to let become fully real.

    She had made certain there was never enough silence for it to settle. As long as there was another fire to contain, another decision to make, another crisis demanding immediate attention, she could keep moving.

    So she kept moving. Solving. Reordering. Placing one problem in front of the next until the day itself became a barricade.

    It had worked, right up until now.

    Now there was nothing left between her and the one problem she had never learned to solve. That miserable excuse for a mother biology had assigned her. The woman who had spent a lifetime confusing cruelty with righteousness.

    Agatha had spent years expecting that particular ghost to return. She simply hadn't expected her to announce herself with a corpse.

    Then again...

    Perhaps she should have.

    The old zealot had already tried to destroy the one thing her fallen child valued more than herself. Sabotaging Nicky's adoption should have settled any remaining illusions. This had never been about revenge. Revenge eventually ended.

    What Evanora wanted was obedience.

    She had spent Agatha's entire life trying to force her into the same shape: smaller, quieter, easier to rule.

    Every ambition she had ever nurtured. Every happiness she had ever managed to build. Every piece of herself she had refused to surrender. Sooner or later, that bigot who mistook fanaticism for parenting reached for all of it. Not because she wanted it. Because it mattered to the abomination she'd created.

    That was how her mother fought. She rarely opened with the killing blow. She preferred finding the first loose thread, giving it the gentlest possible tug, then standing back while everyone else unraveled the tapestry for her.

    Only once the ending had become inevitable did she return.

    That fanatic liked witnessing the decay.

    One dead executive.

    One investigation nudged into motion at precisely the right angle.

    That was all it took.

    S.H.I.E.L.D. would arrive convinced it had uncovered a conspiracy.

    Executives would protect themselves.

    Competitors would smell blood.

    Investors would quietly begin recalculating risk.

    Every one of them believing they were responding to events. None of them realizing they were merely completing someone else's design.

    That had always been Evanora's gift: she understood that competent people rarely needed to be manipulated, only persuaded they were acting of their own accord. She pushed and arranged.

    Entropy did the rest.

    That was the only force Agatha had never learned to negotiate with. The invisible accumulation of microscopic shifts until a structure that had seemed permanent suddenly remembered it had been falling apart for years.

    The architect of her traumatic childhood counted on it.

    She also knew exactly where to apply that pressure.

    Her impure daughter occupied the quiet intersection where politics, organized crime, entertainment, and money overlapped. Every one of those worlds depended on the same invisible assumption: Agatha Harkness remained in control.

    If the first domino Evanora had tipped that morning kept falling, entropy would accomplish what no rival, no federal agency, and no criminal organization ever had. It would make THE Agatha Harkness look fallible. Ordinary. Human.

    Agatha had spent years convincing herself that particular instinct, the habit of arranging the board before making the final move, belonged to someone else.

    It didn't.

    There would be time to resent the inheritance later.

    She drew one slow breath, stepped out of the car, and crossed the garage without breaking stride.

    The elevator rose.

    When the doors opened, the child still hiding somewhere inside her stayed behind. The Reaper of Westview walked out.

    The transformation was seamless.

    Competence.

    Authority.

    The quiet implication that disappointing her might prove hazardous to one's career. The building noticed before anyone else.

    Conversations shortened as she approached. Assistants adjusted course. Lighting technicians stepped aside. Sound engineers instinctively cleared her path. Servers flattened themselves against the walls without quite realizing why. Security acknowledged her with the discreet familiarity reserved for people whose authority had stopped requiring confirmation years ago. Nobody stared.

    Experience had taught everyone the same lesson.

    If the Head Producer was walking quickly, somebody else was probably about to have a very difficult evening.

    She moved through the backstage corridors as though she'd designed them herself. Hollywood, after all, was nothing more than architecture built from perception. And nobody understood illusion better than the woman who built careers out of it. Her assistant intercepted her beside the private entrance leading toward the restricted production corridors. An iPad rested against his chest beside his tablet, both held with the protective caution of devices already containing far too many expensive problems. Without breaking stride, she handed him her evening bag. He accepted it automatically and passed her the iPad in the same motion.

    “One sponsor suddenly has ethical concerns he somehow didn't have yesterday” he began, matching her pace. "Distribution wants revisions to language Legal already approved. Security picked up two unauthorized photographers near the east entrance. The gala host has food poisoning, which means your press obligations just doubled, and Mr. Spector says he won't do interviews unless…"

    “Remind Mr. Spector he’s under contract with Westview for three more seasons.” The lacquer-red soles of her heels disappeared soundlessly into the ugly but meticulously maintained theater carpet as they passed a windowless office marked ACCESS RESTRICTED.

    “Three seasons during which I retain significant influence over how essential his character remains to the story”

    Herbert nodded.

    "And if professionalism fails to inspire him, and it will, mention that the afterparty guest list remains flexible"

    A corner of Herbert's mouth twitched.

    “That should help him rediscover his passion for his profession”

    "Yes, ma'am"

    The relief in his voice was almost touching.

    * Imagine living in a world where Marc Spector qualified as an emergency. That might have been the easiest problem she'd encountered all day. *

    In all honesty, the screening itself barely qualified as work. The real work happened afterward. Behind closed doors. Off the record. In conversations where favors were exchanged, alliances quietly renewed, and the occasional reminder delivered that protection remained conditional while loyalty always carried a price tag.

    Normally, that schedule would have been merely exhausting.

    Tonight it had to fit inside the shrinking stretch of hours separating the premiere from the obscenely early flight Elektra had arranged beneath three separate aliases and a travel history intentionally designed to resist reconstruction.

    Agatha, therefore, cut directly to logistics.

    “I’ll do press before the screening only”

    Another restricted door unlocked with a hydraulic sigh.

    "Keep it to Westview outlets and journalists whose professional interests already align with ours."

    "Understood"

    “Who’s first?”

    “A podcaster” Herbert pushed the last door. “She’s already at the interview setup.” One world ended cleanly at the threshold.

    Behind them, the apparatus of the event continued unchanged: fluorescent light, service corridors, crew members moving with the precise urgency of people trained never to panic.Ahead, the illusion everyone had come to maintain waited intact. Red light washed across marble and glass, turning expensive surfaces into something that almost resembled self-illumination. Velvet ropes divided the lobby into hierarchies nobody acknowledged out loud. The air carried traces of perfume, champagne, and money spent defensively. Laughter, carefully moderated, drifted between clusters of guests. Beyond the glass façade, camera flashes fractured the night while fans pressed against barricades and publicists guided actors from mark to mark with the concentration of air- traffic controllers directing unusually attractive aircraft.

    Agatha surveyed the room once.

    Nothing worth correcting.

    Premieres were never celebrations.

    They were confidence exercises.

    Studios reassured investors.

    Advertisers reassured shareholders.

    Audiences reassured themselves that somewhere beneath the couture, the interviews, and the sponsorship deals, somebody still cared about the work.

    By the time most productions reached a room like this, unpredictability had already been negotiated out of them.

    The rough edges had been sanded smooth.

    The inconvenient instincts focus-grouped into obedience.

    Hollywood rarely sold stories.

    It sold certainty.

    Darkhold had refused.

    It began exactly as Agatha intended: commercially viable, distinctive enough to stand apart, familiar enough to sell.

    Another product.

    Preferably an obscenely profitable one.

    Somewhere between the rewrites, the delays, the emergency reshoots, and the offensive amount of money quietly disappearing into places its producer preferred not to examine too closely, it stopped feeling like inventory.

    It became something she wanted to protect.

    She could never identify the precise moment that happened.

    Only the fact that it had.

    Looking back, inviting Rio anywhere near the writers' room had probably been the original accounting error.

    Her favorite conflict of interest possessed an almost supernatural talent for refusing to let things remain simple.

    Stories became stranger.

    People became more honest than they intended.

    Problems acquired unnecessary emotional depth.

    She had a habit of pulling at whatever was most interesting until it stopped behaving the way everyone expected.

    Life received exactly the same treatment.

    Negotiations became personal.

    Friendships became loyalties.

    Arguments became foreplay.

    Disasters became stories worth telling.

    She moved through Hollywood, and through the rest of existence, with the serene confidence of someone who had never seriously considered the possibility that reality might refuse her anything she genuinely wanted.

    Against all available evidence, reality usually surrendered.

    Agatha had watched that confidence derail negotiations, destroy production schedules, trigger spectacular shutdowns and, on one memorably expensive occasion, reduce an Aston Martin to an insurance claim.

    Which explained why that crisis generator occupied the final line on tonight's agenda. Everything else could be handled through ordinary means.

    Money.

    Influence.

    Information.

    Threats.

    Rio required strategy.

    Because, much as it offended Agatha to admit it, her obscenely wealthy excuse for a business partner had been right.

    Anyone accustomed to reading people would eventually notice the contradiction. Rio Vidal officially occupied no place in Agatha Harkness's life.

    Certainly none inside her empire.

    By every observable measure, she should have disappeared months ago; another cautionary tale traded between ambitious people working the darker corners of Los Angeles. Instead, she remained.

    Writing.

    Laughing.

    Entirely too alive.

    Entirely too comfortable treating Hollywood's hidden crime overlord with the casual irreverence most people reserved for close friends or imminent death. In a city built on greed, vice, and professional predation, anomalies rarely stayed invisible. Sooner or later, someone would conclude that Rio mattered.

    The moment they did, she would stop being interesting.

    She would become useful.

    And Agatha, the woman who had placed her squarely inside that orbit, was about to leave the city.

    That reduced the evening to a single remaining obligation: She had to speak to Rio. Before Wanda arrived and the night stopped belonging to her.

    The only complication was that conversations traditionally required both participants. And that walking natural disaster had spent months making her opinion of face-to-face conversations perfectly clear. Agatha had respected that preference. Tonight, she couldn't afford to.

    Experience had taught her that disappearing without explanation demanded far too much of Rio's imagination.

    She interpreted absence as rejection.

    Rejection as abandonment.

    Everything after that escalated with alarming creativity.

    There was, admittedly, an adult solution.

    Invite that beautifully ungovernable woman somewhere private. Explain the situation. Answer every obvious question before she invented better ones.

    No omissions or riddles. No tactical half-truths.

    Objectively, an excellent plan.

    Its only meaningful flaw was that it required Agatha to communicate like a well-adjusted human being.

    She would sooner drag herself barefoot across Sunset Boulevard.

    That left her with one reliable language.

    Seduction.

    Morally questionable.

    Operationally flawless.

    Coincidentally, Maybelline's spectacular attempt to extort another budget increase from Lady Death had recently confirmed one particularly useful fact.

    Rio was still desperate to fuck her.

    Normally that knowledge would've been satisfying.

    Tonight, it was operational.

    As that arsonist's former owner (and, for all practical purposes, still her current one) she knew Rio too well.

    Reason rarely worked on her.

    Neither did direct orders, common sense, or even basic self-preservation. Desire, however...

    Desire answered to different laws.

    Agatha had never found a compelling reason to stop taking advantage of that particular weakness.

    That made tonight's wardrobe considerably less fashionable than tactical. Premieres belonged to couture. Rio belonged to tailoring. Months of extraordinarily irresponsible field research had settled the matter beyond dispute.

    The tuxedo was the invitation.

    The lace beneath it was the negotiation.

    She only needed a few uninterrupted minutes. Long enough to remind that troubled puppy whose hand still held the leash, and that freedom had always sounded considerably better than it actually felt.

    After that, impossibility could resume its normal business hours.

    First, however, came the tedious part.

    Remaining visible.

    Smiling on cue.

    Exchanging expensive pleasantries with people who mistook networking for personality. In fact…

    "Hey, Harkness"

    The voice belonged to a man standing in the precise stretch of floor she intended to cross. He held a luminous red cocktail and wore the overrehearsed ease of someone who had spent too many years hearing his own opinions echoed back as consensus.

    “If the show’s half as good as this” he said warmly, lifting the glass “you’re about to own television.”

    She searched her memory.

    Nothing. Not even the faintest flicker of recognition.

    Herbert caught the blank look and leaned in without being asked.

    “Daniel Rand" he murmured. "Self-appointed mindfulness guru."

    When that still failed to produce recognition, he kept going.

    "Family money. Wellness entrepreneur. He pitched us that meditation series." Recognition arrived.

    Not of the man.

    Of the rejection.

    "Mr. Rand." Her smile arrived a fraction of a second later than it should have, yet exactly where intended. "It's been a while."

    He beamed As she spoke, two fingers brushed Herbert's forearm.

    Brief.

    Almost imperceptible.

    A perfectly measured acknowledgment.

    He understood.

    The human piggy bank drifted closer for Hollywood's preferred version of intimacy: an air kiss delivered without interrupting the steady flow of compliments somehow lavish enough to sound expensive and empty enough to mean absolutely nothing.

    “The place looks incredible.”

    Agatha stopped listening shortly after that.

    Tiny flecks of crimson glitter clung to the corners of his mouth.

    Every smile caught them briefly against his teeth.

    It was an unfortunate detail to notice.

    Worse, once noticed, it became impossible to ignore.

    Fortunately, the ordeal proved brief.

    "Oh. Hold on." Rand interrupted himself mid-sentence, his attention dropping to her empty hand. "No. That feels cosmically unbalanced"

    Before she could object, he veered toward a passing server balancing a silver tray crowded with identical glowing cocktails.

    Agatha glanced at Herbert.

    "Who approved the radioactive cough syrup?"

    "Mrs. Jones personally signed off on the immersive cocktail program three months ago, ma'am."

    That earned it.

    The cackle escaped before she could stop it.

    Loud.

    Genuine.

    The sort of inappropriate laugh that sounded as though it had broken out of solitary confinement.

    Rand stopped mid-reach.

    The server flinched.

    Two nearby publicists physically jumped.

    Half the lobby looked over.

    * Death had done remarkably little to curb Dottie Jones's instinct for micromanagement * Rand returned triumphantly with the luminous cocktail. Too late. Herbert had already placed a glass of champagne into Agatha's hand.

    She took it without looking.

    Because something far more interesting had just entered her field of vision. Rio.

    Standing across the lobby like a beautifully expensive mistake.

    Gold clung to her body in a gown that appeared to have lost a prolonged argument with modesty.

    Bare shoulders.

    Endless legs.

    Her hair swept up, exposing the delicate line of her neck and the familiar constellation of ink Agatha could have traced blindfolded.

    Rings flashed across nearly every finger she wore, catching the light in brief metallic glints that, from a distance, looked almost like the flicker of a knife changing hands. And then there was the smile.

    That infuriating little gap between her front teeth, just enough to ruin the elegance of the entire look by making it unmistakably Rio.

    She looked pleased. Too pleased.

    Good.

    That could only mean the troublesome little thing had missed their little games just as much as she had.

    Agatha's fingers drifted to the single button fastening her tuxedo jacket. She undid it.

    Let the jacket fall open.

    * Let's play, sweetheart. *
